docs.title: 实验12：添加系统调用异常支持
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》7.1.1 实践任务12：添加系统调用异常支持

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 为 CPU 添加 CSR 寄存器和 CSR 访问指令，实现 syscall 系统调用异常与 ertn 返回，支持"陷入—处理—返回"的完整闭环。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实验十一实现的CPU基础上完成以下工作：

  • 为CPU增加CSR访问指令：csrrd、csrwr、csrxchg、ertn。
  • 为CPU增加控制状态寄存器：CRMD、PRMD、ESTAT、ERA、EENTRY、SAVE0~3。
  • 为CPU增加syscall指令，实现系统调用异常支持。

精确异常

异常响应要求：异常发生时，ERA 记录触发指令的 PC，ESTAT 记录异常编码（syscall 为 Ecode 0x0B），特权级切换到 PLV0，PC 跳转到 EENTRY；ertn 从 ERA 恢复返回。流水线中可能同时有多条指令带异常标志，必须保证"异常前的指令效果生效、异常后的指令不生效"。

测试程序请选择EXP12

docs.text:
1. 将所实现CPU的代码更新至mycpu_env/myCPU/目录中。
  2. 修改func配置文件——mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h，选择exp12的配置，编译。（make EXP=12）
  3. 打开gettrace 工程——mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr。运行gettrace 工程的仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all等待仿真运行完成），生成新的参考trace文件golden_trace.txt（mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt）。要等仿真运行完成，golden_trace.txt才有完整的内容。
  4. 进入 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_bram/run_vivado/ 目录下启动验证myCPU的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。如果该目录下已有前一实践任务创建过的工程，可以在打开工程后，更新项目中CPU实现文件的列表。

docs.text:

实现提示

  • 各 CSR 的地址与各域的含义以LoongArch32R指令集手册为准；
  • csrwr 写入新值的同时要把旧值返回给 rd；csrxchg 按 rj 的掩码逐位交换；

原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》7.1.2 实践任务13：添加其它异常支持

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 为 CPU 添加更多异常和中断的支持，完善精确异常框架。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实验十二实现的CPU基础上完成以下工作：

  • 为CPU增加异常支持：取指地址错乱（ADEF）、地址非对齐（ALE）、断点（BRK）、指令不存在（INE）。
  • 为CPU增加中断支持：包括 2 个软件中断、8 个硬件中断和定时器中断。
  • 为CPU增加控制状态寄存器：ECFG、BADV、TID、TCFG、TVAL、TICLR。
  • 为CPU增加读取计数器指令：rdcntvl.w、rdcntvh.w、rdcntid。

中断的引入时机

中断是异步事件，但响应必须选择指令间隙：不打断已进入流水线的指令。常用做法是在取指时伴随指令打上"携带中断"标志，该指令提交时若中断仍有效则按异常响应，其后指令被冲刷。中断的使能与屏蔽由 CRMD.IE、ECFG.LIE 与 ESTAT.IS 共同决定。

  5. 对工程中的inst_ram重新定制。
  6. 在验证myCPU的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  7. 在验证myCPU的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.text:

实现提示

  • 各异常的检测位置不同：ADEF 在取指时、INE/BRK 在译码时、ALE 在访存时（ALE 还要把出错地址记入 BADV）。异常标志需随流水级传递，在提交点按指令序仲裁；
  • 定时器：TCFG 配置定时器并选择周期，TVAL 反映当前计数值，TICLR 用于清定时器中断。

docs.title: AXI总线接口
docs.text:
请先阅读《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》相关章节的讲解部分，再返回当前实验讲义阅读实验要求并完成。

Warning

所有实验要求请以当前实验讲义为准，请不要参考《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》中的实验要求！

原书参考

本栏实验对应《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》第 8 章 AXI总线接口设计。

真实系统中，CPU 并不直接连着存储器，而是通过总线协议与外界交互。本栏从自定义的类 SRAM 总线过渡到 AXI 协议，并引入随机延迟验证。

docs.title: 实验14：添加类SRAM总线支持
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》8.1.1 实践任务14：添加类SRAM总线支持

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 将 CPU 对外的 SRAM 接口改造为类SRAM总线接口（带握手机制），使 CPU 能够容忍访存等待。

docs.title: 环境介绍
docs.text:
Warning

本实验的验证环境不再使用 soc_bram/ 子目录，而应使用 soc_hs_bram/ 子目录！

伴随着CPU访问的指令RAM和数据RAM从普通的block RAM更换为带握手机制的block RAM，验证环境相应调整：gettrace/、func/ 和 myCPU/ 子目录的位置和用途依然维持不变，只是 soc_verify/ 子目录下改用 soc_hs_bram/ 子目录，其文件组织结构与 soc_bram/ 相似：

|--mycpu_env/                实验环境根目录
|--gettrace/                 生成参考trace的部分。
|--func/                     实验任务所用的功能验证测试程序。
|--myCPU/                    自己实现的CPU的RTL代码。
|--soc_verify/               自己实现的CPU的SoC系统验证环境
   |--soc_hs_bram/           CPU对外连接handshaking block RAM接口时对应的验证环境。
      |--rtl/                SoC_Lite设计代码目录。
      |  |--soc_lite_top.v   SoC_Lite的顶层文件。
      |  |--CONFREG/         confreg模块，用于访问CPU与开发板上数码管、拨码开关等外设。
      |  |--BRIDGE/          1×2的桥接模块，CPU的data sram接口同时访问confreg和data_ram。
      |  |--ram_wrap/        以类SRAM接口封装的RAM模块。
      |  |--xilinx_ip/       定制的Xilinx IP，包含clk_pll、inst_ram、data_ram。
      |--testbench/          功能仿真验证平台。
      |  |--mycpu_tb.v       功能仿真顶层，该模块会抓取debug信息与golden_trace.txt进行比对。
      |--run_vivado/         Vivado工程的运行目录。
         |--constraints/     Vivado工程的设计约束。
         |--mycpu_hs_bram_prj/ Vivado工程文件所在目录。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实验十三实现的CPU基础上完成以下工作：

  • 将CPU对外接口修改为类SRAM总线接口：在原有 sram 接口信号的基础上增加 inst_sram_addr_ok、inst_sram_data_ok、data_sram_addr_ok、data_sram_data_ok 握手信号。请求发出后可能要等待多拍才能得到应答，CPU 流水线必须能在等待期间正确冻结。
  • 在采用握手机制的block RAM的SoC验证环境中完成 exp14 对应func的随机延迟功能验证。

随机延迟

验证环境中的 RAM 访问延迟是随机的（由 confreg.v 中的伪随机数发生器生成）。仿真时初始随机种子由 confreg.v 里的宏 RANDOM_SEED 指定；上板时由复位期间采样到的拨码开关状态指定。请确认你的 CPU 在任意延迟下都能正确工作。

测试程序请选择EXP14

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 将所实现CPU的代码更新至mycpu_env/myCPU/目录中。
  2. 修改func配置文件——mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h，选择exp14的配置，编译。（make EXP=14）
  3. 打开gettrace 工程——mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr。运行gettrace 工程的仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all等待仿真运行完成），生成新的参考trace文件golden_trace.txt（mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt）。要等仿真运行完成，golden_trace.txt才有完整的内容。
  4. 进入 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_hs_bram/run_vivado/ 目录下启动验证myCPU的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。
  5. 对工程中的inst_ram重新定制。
  6. 在验证myCPU的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  7. 在验证myCPU的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。
上板验证要求

上板验证时，要求"随意切换拨码开关后按复位键"，CPU能通过对应exp14的func中58个功能点的验证。

复位期间的拨码开关状态作为初始随机种子，决定取指和访存的随机延迟拍数。不同种子下 CPU 执行状态差别很大，某个种子下出错是很常见的。若出现"仿真通过、上板不过"，可将 confreg.v 中的 RANDOM_SEED 改为出错的种子值再仿真复现调试。上板时应尽量覆盖长延迟、短延迟、无延迟三类延迟（种子与延迟类型的对应关系参见原书图8.1）。

复位后拨码开关的第二个功能是控制数码管的累加速度（调整测试观察节奏）。

docs.text:
• 实验14 测试程序（n1~n58，共58个功能点）仿真PASS。
  • 上板两个双色LED全为绿色，数码管显示"3A00 003A"，且更换多个随机种子（多次切换拨码开关+复位）均能通过。

docs.title: 实验16：完成AXI随机延迟验证
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》8.1.3 实践任务16：完成AXI随机延迟验证

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 完善AXI总线接口设计，在随机总线延迟下验证 CPU 功能与握手的健壮性。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实验十五实现的CPU基础上完成以下工作：

完善AXI总线接口设计，使其在采用AXI总线的SoC验证环境里完成 exp16 对应func的随机延迟功能验证，要求成功通过仿真和上板验证。

为什么随机延迟能抓出 bug

固定延迟的应答掩盖了握手时序问题：READY 迟到、VALID 撤销时机错误、多拍等待中丢数据等 bug，只有延迟随机化后才会暴露。随机延迟由 confreg.v 中的伪随机数发生器生成，仿真时其初始种子由宏 RANDOM_SEED 控制。

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 将所实现CPU的代码更新至mycpu_env/myCPU/目录中。
  2. 修改func配置文件——mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h，选择exp16的配置，编译。（make EXP=16）
  3. 打开gettrace 工程——mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr。运行gettrace 工程的仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all等待仿真运行完成），生成新的参考trace文件golden_trace.txt（mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt）。要等仿真运行完成，golden_trace.txt才有完整的内容。
  4. 进入 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/run_vivado/ 目录下启动验证myCPU的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。
  5. 对工程中的axi_ram重新定制。
  6. 修改 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/rtl/CONFREG/confreg.v 文件中宏 RANDOM_SEED 为不同值，在验证myCPU的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  7. 重复上一步骤多次，要求宏 RANDOM_SEED 的修改值能覆盖三种随机延迟类型（长延迟、短延迟、无延迟）。
  8. 在验证myCPU的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.title: 验收标准
docs.text:
• 实验16 测试程序（n1~n58，共58个功能点）仿真PASS，且覆盖三种延迟类型的多组 RANDOM_SEED 均通过。
  • 上板两个双色LED全为绿色，数码管显示"3A00 003A"。
上板验证要求

上板验证时，要求"随意切换拨码开关后按复位键"均能正确运行func（复位期间的拨码开关状态作为初始随机种子）。如果出现"仿真通过，上板不过"的现象，请按照实验十四介绍的方法进行调试：将出错的种子写入 confreg.v 的 RANDOM_SEED 后仿真复现；无法复现时，排查代码规范性问题或使用 Vivado 逻辑分析仪在线调试。

docs.title: 存储管理单元（TLB）
docs.text:
请先阅读《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》相关章节的讲解部分，再返回当前实验讲义阅读实验要求并完成。

Warning

所有实验要求请以当前实验讲义为准，请不要参考《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》中的实验要求！

原书参考

本栏实验对应《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》第 9 章 存储管理单元设计。

操作系统需要虚拟地址：进程隔离、按需调页、共享内存都靠它。MMU 负责虚实地址转换，核心部件是 TLB（Translation Lookaside Buffer）。

本栏先做出独立的 TLB 模块，再把 TLB 指令、CSR、例外接入 CPU。

docs.title: 实验17：TLB模块设计
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》9.1 TLB模块设计分析 / 9.2.1 实践任务17：TLB模块设计

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 设计并实现独立的 TLB 模块，完成模块级验证。

docs.title: 环境介绍
docs.text:
Warning

本实验的验证环境与之前的SoC环境不同，是针对TLB模块的单独验证环境，位于 mycpu_env/module_verify/tlb_verify/ 目录下，不使用 func 测试。

|--module_verify/            模块级验证环境
   |--tlb_verify/            TLB模块级验证环境。
      |--rtl/                包含TLB模块以及验证顶层的设计源码。
      |  |--tlb_top.v        TLB模块级验证的顶层文件。
      |--testbench/          功能仿真验证源码。
      |  |--testbench.v      仿真顶层。
      |--run_vivado/         Vivado工程的运行目录。
         |--constraints/     Vivado工程的设计约束。
         |--tlb_prj/         Vivado工程文件所在目录。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求如下：

  • 设计TLB模块，RTL文件记为 tlb.v，模块名必须命名为 tlb，输入/输出端口参考原书 9.1 节的接口定义（两套查找端口、TLBSRCH 查找、TLBWR/TLBFILL 写端口、TLBRD 读端口、INVTLB 操作）。
  • 利用TLB模块级验证环境对所设计的TLB进行验证，通过仿真和上板验证。

设计要点

  • 查找采用全相联并行比较：所有表项同时与输入的 VPPN/ASID 比较，生成 match 向量；命中项的信息经多路选择输出；
  • 比较条件要兼顾 G 位（全局项忽略 ASID）与页大小（4MB 页只比较高 10 位 VPPN，4KB 页比较全部 19 位）；
  • 表项数建议 16 项（parameter TLBNUM = 16）。

使用 Chisel BlackBox 对齐顶层

用 BlackBox 引用 tlb.v，端口名与 module tlb 逐字对齐，clk/rst 显式声明并连接；必要时用 HasBlackBoxResource 引入 Verilog 源文件。

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 完成TLB模块的设计和RTL编写，记为tlb.v，将tlb.v文件放入mycpu_env/myCPU/ 目录下。
  2. 进入 mycpu_env/module_verify/tlb_verify/run_vivado/tlb_prj/ 目录下启动验证tlb的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。
  3. 在验证tlb模块的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  4. 在验证tlb模块的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.title: 验收标准
docs.text:
• TLB模块级仿真PASS（共 16 次写、16 次读以及 26 次查找操作，全部正确后打印 PASS!!!）。
  • TLB模块上板正确。
仿真验证结果判断

在仿真时，会有16次写，16次读以及26次查操作，所有操作都完成后会打印PASS，如下所示：

    [   2705 ns] OK!!!write
    …………
    =========================================================
    Test end!
    ----PASS!!!
如果仿真中发现错误，请进行调试。这时需要观察TLB接口的访问，了解该次请求的效果，然后查看TLB的读出数据是否与预期效果相同。

上板验证结果判断

上板运行时数码管会依次反映各阶段进度：

  1. 写操作（W）：最右侧数码管从 0x00 累加到 0x0f，完成后最右侧单色 LED 亮起；
  2. 读（R）与查找（S0/S1）同时进行：次右侧数码管（R）从 0x00 加到 0x0f；次左侧数码管（S0，偶数次请求）以步长 2 从 0x00 加到 0x18；最左侧数码管（S1，奇数次请求）以步长 2 从 0x01 加到 0x19；
  3. 全部完成后 LED 右侧三个灯亮起，正确结束时数码管显示 0x19180f0f。停在其它数值表示上板失败。

docs.title: 实验18：添加TLB相关指令和CSR寄存器
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》9.2.2 实践任务18：添加TLB相关指令和CSR寄存器

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 将实验十七完成的TLB模块集成到CPU中，添加TLB相关指令和CSR寄存器。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实验十六和实验十七的基础上完成以下工作：

  • 将实践任务17完成的TLB模块集成到实践任务16完成的CPU中。
  • 在CPU中增加TLB操作指令：TLBSRCH、TLBRD、TLBWR、TLBFILL、INVTLB。
  • 在CPU中增加CSR寄存器：TLBIDX、TLBEHI、TLBELO0、TLBELO1、ASID、TLBRENTRY。

测试程序请选择EXP18

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 将所实现CPU的代码更新至mycpu_env/myCPU/目录中。
  2. 修改func配置文件——mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h，选择exp18的配置，编译。（make EXP=18）
  3. 打开gettrace 工程——mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr。运行gettrace 工程的仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all等待仿真运行完成），生成新的参考trace文件golden_trace.txt（mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt）。要等仿真运行完成，golden_trace.txt才有完整的内容。
  4. 进入 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/run_vivado/ 目录下启动验证myCPU的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。如果该目录下已有前一实践任务创建过的工程，可以在打开工程后，更新项目中CPU实现文件的列表。
  5. 对工程中的axi_ram重新定制。
  6. 在验证myCPU的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  7. 在验证myCPU的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.title: 验收标准
docs.text:
• 实验18 测试程序（n1~n70，共70个功能点）仿真PASS。
  • 上板两个双色LED全为绿色，数码管显示"4600 0046"。

实现提示

  • 五条 TLB 指令的操作数与结果都通过 CSR 传递（TLBEHI 放待查 VPPN、TLBELO0/1 放表项内容、TLBIDX 放表项号与查询结果），CSR→TLB、TLB→CSR 两条通路都要接好；
  • 本实验还不需要实现虚实地址转换——CPU 仍工作在直接映射模式，func 测试验证的是指令与 CSR 本身的正确性。

docs.title: 实验19：添加TLB相关例外支持
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》9.2.3 实践任务19：添加TLB相关例外支持

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 为 CPU 添加 TLB 相关例外与虚实地址映射功能，完成 MMU 的全部功能。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实验十八所实现CPU的基础上完成以下工作：

  • 为CPU增加TLB相关异常：TLB重填例外、load/store/取指操作页无效例外、页修改例外、页特权等级不合规例外。
  • 在CPU中增加DMW CSR寄存器。
  • 为CPU增加虚实地址映射的功能。

地址翻译模式

CRMD 的 DA/PG 域决定翻译模式：直接映射（DA=1）时按 DMW 寄存器配置直接映射；页映射（PG=1）时虚地址先查 TLB 得到 PPN 再拼物理地址。TLB 例外的检测位置在取指（IF）和访存（MEM），比 syscall 等更靠前也更频繁，要把它们纳入实验十二/十三建立的精确异常仲裁框架。

测试程序请选择EXP19

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 将所实现CPU的代码更新至mycpu_env/myCPU/目录中。
  2. 修改func配置文件——mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h，选择exp19的配置，编译。（make EXP=19）
  3. 打开gettrace 工程——mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr。运行gettrace 工程的仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all等待仿真运行完成），生成新的参考trace文件golden_trace.txt（mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt）。要等仿真运行完成，golden_trace.txt才有完整的内容。
  4. 进入 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/run_vivado/ 目录下启动验证myCPU的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。如果该目录下已有前一实践任务创建过的工程，可以在打开工程后，更新项目中CPU实现文件的列表。
  5. 对工程中的axi_ram重新定制。
  6. 在验证myCPU的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  7. 在验证myCPU的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.title: 验收标准
docs.text:
• 实验19 测试程序（n1~n72，共72个功能点）仿真PASS。
  • 上板两个双色LED全为绿色，数码管显示"4800 0048"。

实现提示

  • 各例外的区分：TLB 查找 miss → 重填例外；命中但 V=0 → 页无效例外（还要区分取指/取数来源）；store 命中但 D=0 → 页修改例外；当前 PLV 低于表项 PLV → 特权等级不合规例外；
  • 触发例外的虚地址记入 TLBRBADV（区别于通用的 BADV）；
  • 例外的入口地址（EENTRY 或专设的 TLB 重填入口）与 ertn 恢复 DA/PG 的行为，请对照LoongArch32R指令集手册实现。

docs.title: 高速缓存（Cache）
docs.text:
请先阅读《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》相关章节的讲解部分，再返回当前实验讲义阅读实验要求并完成。

Warning

所有实验要求请以当前实验讲义为准，请不要参考《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》中的实验要求！

原书参考

本栏实验对应《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》第 10 章 高速缓存设计。

CPU 与主存的速度差距以数量级计，Cache 用局部性原理加速CPU速度，减少等待主存数据时CPU阻塞的时间。

本栏先实现独立的 Cache 模块（含 AXI 总线接口与未命中处理状态机），再把 ICache、DCache 集成进 CPU，并添加 CACOP 指令维护。

docs.title: 实验20：Cache模块设计
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》10.1 Cache模块的设计 / 10.2.1 实践任务20：Cache模块设计

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 设计并实现独立的 Cache 模块，完成模块级验证。

docs.title: 环境介绍
docs.text:
Warning

本实验的验证环境与SoC环境不同，是针对Cache模块的单独验证环境，位于 mycpu_env/module_verify/cache_verify/ 目录下，不使用 func 测试。

|--module_verify/            模块级验证环境
   |--cache_verify/          Cache模块级验证环境。
      |--rtl/                包含Cache模块以及验证顶层的设计源码。
      |  |--cache_top.v      Cache模块级验证的顶层文件。
      |--testbench/          功能仿真验证源码。
      |  |--testbench.v      仿真顶层。
      |--run_vivado/         Vivado工程的运行目录。
         |--constraints/     Vivado工程的设计约束。
         |--cache_prj/       Vivado工程文件所在目录。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务的要求如下：

  • 设计Cache模块，RTL文件记为 cache.v，模块名必须命名为 cache。除时钟输入 clk 和低电平有效复位输入 resetn 以外，输入/输出端口参考原书 10.1 节表 10.2（与CPU流水线的类SRAM交互）和表 10.3（与AXI总线接口模块的读写交互）中的定义。
  • 设计规格要求：2路组相联，每路大小4KB，Cache行16字节，LRU或伪随机替换算法，推荐硬件初始化。
  • 利用Cache模块级验证环境对所设计的Cache进行验证，通过仿真和上板验证。

设计要点

  • 地址划分：虚地址 [11:4] 作 Index（8位），物理地址 [31:12] 作 Tag（20位），行内偏移 4 位——即"虚Index实Tag"（VIPT）访问方式；
  • Cache RAM 需要自行定制：TAGV RAM 256×21 共 2 块；DATA Bank RAM 256×32 共 8 块（需开启字节写使能；定制时不要勾选 "Primitives Output Register"，保证单周期返回）；
  • 内部组织为 4 类访问：Look Up、Hit Write、Replace、Refill，配合主状态机（IDLE/LOOKUP/MISS/REPLACE/REFILL）与写缓冲状态机管理；
  • 数据Cache采用写回+写分配策略；替换出脏行时先经 AXI 写回内存再填入新行。

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 完成Cache模块的设计和RTL编写，记为cache.v，将cache.v文件放入mycpu_env/myCPU/ 目录下。
  2. 进入 mycpu_env/module_verify/cache_verify/run_vivado/cache_prj/ 目录下启动验证cache的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。
  3. 在验证Cache模块的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  4. 在验证Cache模块的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.title: 验收标准
docs.text:
• Cache模块级仿真PASS。
仿真验证结果判断

模块级验证会从index=0的时候开始验证，针对每个index，生成四组随机的tag和data对。首先生成写请求将这四组数写进cache，然后再生成读请求读它们。如果中间没有发生错误，index递增，重新生成tag和data对进行相同的测试，直到index==ff的测试完成为止。

对于写cache请求。验证环境期望看到的结果是，写请求发出后会出现Cache miss，Cache模块会发出rd请求，验证环境返回全1值（0xFFFFFFFF）。写请求可能会引发替换操作，这时验证环境会拿wr_addr和wr_data和前述的tag/data组合做对比，如果replace的值有错，测试会中止。

写操作全部进行完之后会有读操作，验证环境会做同样的检测。当cache返回读操作的结果之后，验证环境会检测读到的结果与之前写入的结果是否相同。

在仿真时，会对每一个index生成四个cache行的先写再读的操作，所有操作都完成后会打印PASS，如下所示：

    [   2705 ns] index 00 finishd
    …………
    =========================================================
    Test end!
    ----PASS!!!
如果在仿真中发现错误，请进行调试，控制台会打印出错误的原因。验证环境只会检查替换时的数据错误和Cache read的数据错误。

上板验证结果判断

上板运行时，数码管的左边两位显示当前测试的 index 值，逐步递增至 0xff 后测试停止。

硬件初始化

由于 CACOP 指令在实验二十三才实现，本阶段的 Cache 初始化需要硬件手段：可在定制 TAGV RAM 时勾选 "Fill Remaining Memory Locations" 并置初始值为 0（V=0 即全无效），D 表用寄存器实现直接复位清零。

docs.title: 实验22：CPU中集成DCache
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》10.2.3 实践任务22：CPU中集成DCache

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 将实验二十完成的Cache模块作为 DCache 集成到CPU访存通路中。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实验二十一完成的基础上完成以下工作：

  • 将实践任务20完成的Cache模块作为DCache集成到实践任务21完成的CPU中。

测试程序请选择EXP22

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 将所实现CPU的代码更新至mycpu_env/myCPU/目录中。
  2. 修改func配置文件——mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h，选择exp22的配置，编译。（make EXP=22）
  3. 打开gettrace 工程——mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr。运行gettrace 工程的仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all等待仿真运行完成），生成新的参考trace文件golden_trace.txt（mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt）。要等仿真运行完成，golden_trace.txt才有完整的内容。
  4. 进入 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/run_vivado/ 目录下启动验证myCPU的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。如果该目录下已有前一实践任务创建过的工程，可以在打开工程后，更新项目中CPU实现文件的列表。
  5. 对工程中的axi_ram重新定制。
  6. 在验证myCPU的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  7. 在验证myCPU的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.title: 验收标准
docs.text:
• 实验22 测试程序（n1~n72，共72个功能点）仿真PASS。
  • 上板两个双色LED全为绿色，数码管显示"4800 0048"。

实现提示

集成 DCache 后，整 CPU 的访存路径变为：流水线 → DCache（类SRAM）→ AXI 转换桥（含 16 字节写缓存与 Burst 读）。建议再次对比运行时间，观察 DCache 的收益。

docs.title: 实验23：CPU中添加CACOP指令
docs.text:
原书参考

《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》10.2.4 实践任务23：CPU中添加CACOP指令

docs.title: 实验目标
docs.text: • 在CPU中实现 CACOP 指令（Cache 维护操作），完成 Cache 实验的最后一环。

docs.title: 实验内容
docs.text:
本实践任务要求在实践任务22完成的基础上完成以下工作：

  • 在实践任务22完成的CPU中增加CACOP指令实现。

CACOP 的语义

cacop op, rj, si12 按 op 值对 rj + sext(si12) 对应 Cache 行（对齐到行边界）执行维护操作：查询（读 Tag 到 CSR）、置无效（清 V，数据丢弃）、写回（脏行写回内存）、冲刷（写回+置无效）。CACOP 是特权指令，非 PLV0 执行触发特权指令例外。

测试程序请选择EXP23

docs.title: 实验步骤
docs.text:
1. 将所实现CPU的代码更新至mycpu_env/myCPU/目录中。
  2. 修改func配置文件——mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h，选择exp23的配置，编译。（make EXP=23）
  3. 打开gettrace 工程——mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr。运行gettrace 工程的仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all等待仿真运行完成），生成新的参考trace文件golden_trace.txt（mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt）。要等仿真运行完成，golden_trace.txt才有完整的内容。
  4. 进入 mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/run_vivado/ 目录下启动验证myCPU的工程。如果该目录下尚未创建工程，请利用该目录下的 create_project.tcl 文件创建工程。如果该目录下已有前一实践任务创建过的工程，可以在打开工程后，更新项目中CPU实现文件的列表。
  5. 对工程中的axi_ram重新定制。
  6. 在验证myCPU的工程中运行仿真（进入仿真界面后，直接点击run all），进行功能验证与调试，直至仿真测试通过。
  7. 在验证myCPU的工程中综合实现后生成bit流文件，进行上板验证。

docs.title: 验收标准
docs.text:
• 实验23 测试程序（n1~n79，共79个功能点）仿真PASS。
  • 上板两个双色LED全为绿色，数码管显示"4F00 004F"。

实现提示

  • 实现了 CACOP 后，Cache 便可以软件初始化：软件用 CACOP 将所有 Tag 置 0 即完成初始化，硬件初始化电路成为备用手段；
  • CACOP 执行期间可能发起总线写回（冲刷脏行），需要像多周期乘除一样冻结流水线等待完成。

docs.title: 介绍
docs.text:
“工欲善其事，必先利其器”，在正式开始实验之前，我们需要进行一些准备工作。

本课程的实验环境由三部分组成：Vivado、WSL2/Linux 环境以及 LoongArch32 交叉编译工具链。

docs.title: Vivado
docs.text:
在实验中应使用版本高于或等于2019.2的Vivado，推荐使用2023.2版本Vivado，能够有效加快仿真和综合实现速度。

详细地Vivado安装教程请参考：Vivado的安装

使用Vivado的小贴士

  • Windows版本Vivado默认2线程编译，可在Tcl Console中输入如下命令：set_param general.maxThreads 8 开启八线程编译加速
  • Linux下Vivado的综合实现速度更快，若有Linux物理机可选择安装Linux版本Vivado
  • 不建议在虚拟机中使用Vivado
  • 工程所在位置的路径不要出现中文，工程所在路径也不应过深，建议直接在磁盘根目录下创建项目
  • 计算机用户名不要使用中文

Vivado 的基本操作（建工程、仿真、上板）可参考原书附录：Vivado使用入门、Vivado使用进阶。

docs.title: WSL2 / Linux 环境
docs.text:
推荐在Windows使用WSL2+Ubuntu，后续实验环境需要在Linux环境下编译测试程序。

安装WSL2+Ubuntu教程请自行查阅。

docs.title: LoongArch32 交叉编译工具链
docs.text:
自行编译func程序需要使用LoongArch32R的GCC交叉编译工具。该工具链的安装可以从 LoongArch32精简版交叉工具链 下安装包。

下载安装包时请根据所用机器是X86还是LoongArch选择对应的版本,以下以X86为例。下载压缩包 loongson-gnu-toolchain-8.3-x86_64-loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-v2.0.tar.xz 至Linux操作系统自身的文件系统中。需要特别提醒的是，目前X86版本LoongArch32R的GCC交叉编译工具只支持64位系统（在系统下运行uname -a命令显示架构为x86_64的）。接下来：

在Linux环境下：

（1）打开一个terminal，进入压缩包所在目录，进行解压： 

sudo tar Jxvf loongson-gnu-toolchain-8.3-x86_64-loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-v2.0.tar.xz -C /opt/

（2）随后执行： 

echo 'export PATH=/opt/loongson-gnu-toolchain-8.3-x86_64-loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-v2.0/bin/:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc && echo $PATH
（3）重新打开一个terminal，查看la32r的gcc交叉编译链版本： 
 loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-gcc -v
若正确输出gcc版本即配置成功。

docs.title: 实验模板
docs.text: 本页介绍如何从 GitHub 获取实验基础模板，以及各目录的结构与用法。开始实验前，请先通读本页。

docs.title: 获取实验模板
docs.text:
本课程实验基于龙芯官方教学实验环境 cdp_ede_local，对龙芯官方实验环境进行了修改，能够在DIGILENT NEXYS 100T开发板上正常运行，修改后的实验环境仓库：cdp_ede_local

首先clone到本地，建议放在windows下，不要放在WSL2中。

git clone git@github.com:zihaojf/cdp_ede_local.git

Tip

建议自己在开发过程中做好版本管理！

克隆完成后，仓库根目录结构如下：

cdp_ede_local/
├── README.md          # 说明文档：实验安排与对应环境
├── dc_env/            # 实验 1~4：数字逻辑电路基础
├── minicpu_env/       # 实验 5：5条指令单周期CPU
└── mycpu_env/         # 实验 6~23：20条指令CPU起的全部实验

三个环境对应课程的三段实验，彼此独立，按实验进度依次使用。

docs.title: dc_env（实验 1~4）
docs.text:
dc_env/
├── exp1/    跑马灯实验
├── exp2/    寄存器堆仿真
├── exp3/    同步/异步 RAM
└── exp4/    数字逻辑电路设计与调试

每个 expN 目录自带源文件骨架、testbench 和约束文件（.xdc），用 Vivado 直接打开或新建工程添加源文件即可。你需要做的是补全/修正源文件，跑通仿真，再综合上板。

docs.title: minicpu_env（实验 5）
docs.text:
minicpu_env/
├── func/           # 测试程序：汇编 → 指令存储器初始化文件
│   ├── start.S         # 斐波那契程序（5条指令即可运行）
│   ├── Makefile        # 交叉编译，产出 inst_ram.coe / inst_ram.txt
│   └── inst_ram.coe    # 编译好的指令镜像（仿真用）
├── miniCPU/        # CPU 的 RTL
│   ├── minicpu_top.v   # 单周期 CPU 顶层
│   ├── regfile.v       # 寄存器堆
│   └── tools.v         # 辅助部件
└── soc_verify/     # SoC 验证环境
    ├── rtl/            # soc_mini_top.v + CONFREG + xilinx_ip
    └── testbench/      # mycpu_tb.v：仿真顶层

已提供一个可运行五条指令的minicpu，在 soc_verify 的 Vivado 工程中运行仿真，CPU 从 inst_ram 取指执行 func 里的斐波那契程序，结果通过 CONFREG（仿真中观察）或数码管（上板）验证。

docs.title: mycpu_env（实验 6~23）
docs.text:
这是课程使用时间最长的环境，后续所有实验都在它上面增量开发。

mycpu_env/
├── myCPU/              # 你的 CPU RTL
│   ├── mycpu_top.v     # CPU 顶层
│   ├── alu.v、regfile.v、decoder_*.v ...
├── func/               # func 功能测试程序集
│   └── inst/           # n1~n79 分项测试汇编（每文件聚焦若干指令）
├── gettrace/           # 参考轨迹生成工具（trace 比对调试用）
├── module_verify/      # 独立模块验证（实验 17 TLB、实验 20 Cache）
│   ├── tlb_verify/     # 实验 17：TLB模块验证
│   ├── cache_verify/   # 实验 20：Cache模块验证
│   ├── mul_verify/     # 乘法器验证
│   ├── div_verify/     # 除法器验证
└── soc_verify/         # SoC 验证环境，按总线接口分四个目录
    ├── soc_dram/       # 实验 6：分布式 RAM 接口（单周期）
    ├── soc_bram/       # 实验 7~13：块 RAM 接口（流水线/异常）
    ├── soc_hs_bram/    # 实验 14：带握手 BRAM 接口
    └── soc_axi/        # 实验 15~23：AXI 总线接口

两点特别注意

  1. myCPU/ 初始代码含有功能错误，这是实验设计的一部分（找错并修正），不是仓库 bug；
  2. 每个实验对应 soc_verify 下不同的 SoC 目录——实验时注意仿真/上板工程用的是哪个目录。

工具链

func/ 的 Makefile 依赖 loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-* 交叉编译工具链（自行编译测试程序时需要）。仿真验证通常只需仓库自带的 inst_ram.coe 镜像，直接跑即可。

docs.title: 实验环境自查清单
docs.text:
开始实验 2 之前，逐项确认：

  • Vivado ≥ 2019.2 安装完成，能新建工程并跑通一个仿真；
  • WSL2/Ubuntu 可用，gcc、make、git 基础工具齐全；
  • LoongArch32 交叉编译工具链安装并加入 PATH；
  • 建立自己的代码仓库

接下来我们将开始实验！

docs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture Labs
docs.text: The goal of the labs in this course is to design a CPU from scratch: starting from basic digital logic components, you will progressively build a five-stage pipelined LoongArch32 CPU that supports more than 20 instructions and provides exception handling, a bus interface, address translation, and a cache — ultimately enabling it to run real C programs and even boot Linux.

docs.title: About the Labs
docs.text:
The instruction set used in this course is the LoongArch32r reduced instruction set. It differs from the RISC-V instruction set taught in the theory lectures, but the two have much in common. If you already understand RISC-V well, learning LoongArch32r will not be difficult.

For the full instruction set reference, see: LoongArch 32-Bit Reduced Instruction Set Reference Manual

The labs in this course accompany CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition (《CPU设计实战：LoongArch版》, by Wang Wenxiang, Hu Wei, and Wang Huandong; China Machine Press).

The electronic edition of this book is sponsored by Loongson Technology and can be read online for free on bookdown.org:

Read the book online

All 23 labs are organized as 8 progressive stages, each building on the results of the previous one:

Stage Book chapter Notes on this site Digital logic fundamentals Chapter 3 labs/01-数字电路基础 (Labs 1–4) Single-cycle CPU Chapter 4 labs/02-单周期CPU设计 (Labs 5–6) Getting started with Chisel —— Getting Started with Chisel Pipelined CPU Chapter 5, Chapter 6 labs/04-流水线CPU设计 (Labs 7–11) Exceptions and interrupts Chapter 7 labs/05-异常与中断 (Labs 12–13) AXI bus interface Chapter 8 labs/06-AXI总线接口 (Labs 14–16) Memory management unit Chapter 9 labs/07-存储管理单元TLB (Labs 17–19) Cache Chapter 10 labs/08-高速缓存Cache (Labs 20–23)

The complete table of contents (including the preface, Chapter 1: Overview of the CPU Chip Development Process, Chapter 3: Fundamentals of Digital Logic Circuit Design, and the appendices) is available in the online edition of the book.

docs.title: Lab Roadmap
docs.text:
The 23 labs build on one another, culminating in a fully functional pipelined CPU:

  • Digital logic fundamentals (Labs 1–4): learn the Vivado simulation, synthesis, and board-programming flow, and independently design and debug basic components such as register files and RAM.
  • Single-cycle CPU (Labs 5–6): implement a single-cycle CPU in Verilog that can execute 20 instructions — the first time a program runs on a processor of your own making.
  • Pipelined CPU (Labs 7–11): switch to Chisel to develop a five-stage pipelined CPU, and resolve data hazards and control hazards in turn (stalling, then forwarding), then extend it with arithmetic/logic, multiply/divide, branch, and memory access instructions.
  • Exceptions, interrupts, the AXI bus, and the TLB (Labs 12–19): add system calls and exception handling to the CPU, upgrade its memory interface to an SRAM-like bus and then an AXI bus, and implement a TLB to perform virtual-to-physical address translation.
  • Adding the cache (Labs 20–23): design a cache module and integrate the ICache and DCache to bridge the speed gap between the processor and main memory. At this point a complete microprocessor is finished.

docs.title: How to Use These Notes
docs.text:
1. Set up your environment before you start: the labs depend on Vivado, a WSL2/Linux environment, and the LoongArch32 cross-compilation toolchain. Read Lab Setup first and complete the installation.

  2. Read the book, then do the lab: before each lab, read the explanatory section of the corresponding chapter of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition. Once you understand the underlying principles, come back to the lab requirements in these notes.

    Warning

    All lab requirements are governed by the lab notes on this site. Do not follow the lab requirements given in CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition!

  3. Make good use of the appendices: if Chisel is new to you, work through Appendix A: Getting Started with Chisel alongside the labs. Before starting the pipeline labs, we recommend reading Appendix B: A Guide to the Five-Stage Pipelined CPU in full to build an overall picture first.

Note

In this course the single-cycle CPU is developed in Verilog and the pipelined CPU in Chisel. The examples in the book are mostly in Verilog, but the design ideas behind the datapath, hazard handling, and exception mechanisms carry over directly, so you can read the book alongside the Chisel notes from this course.

docs.title: Learning Resources
docs.text:
Designing a CPU for the first time can feel daunting. The books and existing open-source processor cores below are useful references:

  1. openLA500 (LoongArch32r, single-issue in-order five-stage pipeline)
  2. openLA1000 (LoongArch32r, three-issue in-order)
  3. NutShell processor (RISC-V, single-issue in-order / multi-issue out-of-order)

docs.title: BlackBox: Wrapping an Existing Verilog Module
docs.text:
The previous chapters all describe hardware from scratch in Chisel. But there are two kinds of things you should not rewrite:

  • Verilog modules that are already written and verified in Vivado, such as tlb.v from Lab 17 and cache.v from Lab 20 of this course;
  • Vendor-supplied IP cores, or the RAMs you customized with Vivado in Labs 1–4.

A BlackBox plugs these modules into the Chisel module hierarchy as they are: Chisel neither translates nor checks their internal logic — it simply emits one instantiation based on the ports you declare.

A BlackBox is not a translator

The inside of a BlackBox is completely invisible to Chisel. The ports you declare are the whole story — if they do not line up, Chisel will not find a way around it; it will simply fail when generating Verilog or during synthesis.

docs.title: When You Need a BlackBox
docs.text:
First, draw the line between a BlackBox and rewriting in Chisel:

Situation Approach The logic is not complex, and you want to keep working on it with Chisel's combinational/sequential facilities Write it directly in Chisel An existing Verilog module with a fixed interface that cannot be changed BlackBox Vendor IP (RAM, PLL, AXI interconnect, and so on) BlackBox You want to hand a Chisel module to Verilog No BlackBox needed — just generate it normally

The key phrase is "fixed interface". Lab 17's tlb.v and Lab 20's cache.v both require the module name, port names, and bit widths to be named exactly as defined in the book (both pages state this outright under "Tasks"), and in that situation wrapping them in a BlackBox is the only option.

docs.title: A Minimal Example
docs.text:
Start with a Verilog module:

module mul_unsigned #(
    parameter WIDTH = 32
) (
    input                    clk,
    input                    resetn,
    input                    start,
    input      [WIDTH-1:0]   a,
    input      [WIDTH-1:0]   b,
    output reg               done,
    output reg [2*WIDTH-1:0] product
);
    // ... 多周期乘法器实现 ...
endmodule

Now write a BlackBox for it in Chisel:

import chisel3._
import chisel3.util.HasBlackBoxPath

class MulUnsigned(width: Int = 32)
    extends BlackBox(Map("WIDTH" -> width))
    with HasBlackBoxPath {

  override def desiredName: String = "mul_unsigned"

  val io = IO(new Bundle {
    val clk     = Input(Clock())
    val resetn  = Input(Bool())
    val start   = Input(Bool())
    val a       = Input(UInt(width.W))
    val b       = Input(UInt(width.W))
    val done    = Output(Bool())
    val product = Output(UInt((2 * width).W))
  })

  addPath("src/main/scala/blackbox/mul_unsigned.v")
}

Item by item:

What you write in Chisel What it corresponds to in Verilog Requirement desiredName the name of the module must match exactly, character for character val clk = Input(Clock()) input clk name and direction match exactly val resetn = Input(Bool()) input resetn as above UInt(width.W) [WIDTH-1:0] bit width matches Map("WIDTH" -> width) parameter WIDTH parameter name matches exactly addPath(...) —— tells Chisel where the source file is

Values in Map(...) are elaboration-time values

The values in a Map can only be Scala Ints or Strings, never a Chisel UInt. Like log2Ceil, they have to be settled when the circuit is generated.

Copy port names verbatim, do not 'tidy them up'

If the Verilog port is called clk, write clk; if it is called resetn, write resetn. This course standardizes on clk / resetn on the Verilog side, which conveniently keeps it distinct from Chisel's implicit clock / reset.

docs.title: You Must Wire Up the Clock and Reset Yourself
docs.text:
A BlackBox does not get its clock and reset inserted automatically — whatever ports you declare, you connect them yourself:

val mul = Module(new MulUnsigned(32))

mul.io.clk    := clock
mul.io.resetn := !reset.asBool    // Chisel 的 reset 是高有效，resetn 是低有效

mul.io.start := start
mul.io.a     := operandA
mul.io.b     := operandB

reset.asBool converts Chisel's Reset into a Bool; since the Verilog side is active-low, the result is then inverted.

Reset polarity

Wiring it the wrong way round raises no error, but the reset never takes effect and large stretches of x will appear in the simulation waveform. If you see x, check this first.

Why connect explicitly instead of relying on the tool

If you name the ports clock / reset they are easily confused with Chisel's implicit clock and reset, while the names on the Verilog side are usually clk / resetn. Declare exactly the real Verilog port names and then connect them explicitly — neither side is ambiguous, and you save yourself the cost of remembering the rules.

docs.title: Ports Are Flat: Use FlatIO
docs.text:
A Verilog port list is flat. If you follow Chisel convention and write a nested Bundle:

// 不推荐：嵌套 Bundle 会生成带下划线拼接的端口名
val io = IO(new Bundle {
  val s0 = new Bundle {              // 会生成 s0_vppn、s0_asid 这样的名字
    val vppn = Input(UInt(19.W))
    val asid = Input(UInt(10.W))
  }
})

The names it produces may just happen to match the Verilog naming, or they may not — it depends on how the field names are joined. Once there are many ports (tlb.v and cache.v both have dozens), this gamble goes wrong easily.

FlatIO is the safer choice: it adds no prefix to port names, so the names are exactly what you write.

class TlbBlackBox extends BlackBox with HasBlackBoxPath {
  override def desiredName: String = "tlb"

  val io = FlatIO(new Bundle {
    val clk    = Input(Clock())
    val resetn = Input(Bool())

    // 查找端口 0（取指）
    val s0_vppn_en  = Input(Bool())
    val s0_vppn     = Input(UInt(19.W))
    val s0_va_bit12 = Input(Bool())
    val s0_asid     = Input(UInt(10.W))
    val s0_found    = Output(Bool())
    val s0_index    = Output(UInt(4.W))
    val s0_ppn      = Output(UInt(20.W))
    // ... 其余端口照抄 tlb.v 逐一写平 ...
  })

  addPath("src/main/scala/blackbox/tlb.v")
}

docs.title: Handing the Source File to Chisel
docs.text:
The addPath above goes together with HasBlackBoxPath, and the path is relative to the Chisel project root:

class AxiBridgeBlackBox extends BlackBox with HasBlackBoxPath {
  override def desiredName: String = "axi_bridge"
  val io = FlatIO(new Bundle { /* ... */ })

  addPath("src/main/scala/blackbox/axi_bridge.v")
  addPath("src/main/scala/blackbox/definition.vh")   // 被 include 的头文件也要加
}

The other option is to put the file under src/main/resources/ and use HasBlackBoxResource + addResource:

import chisel3.util.HasBlackBoxResource

class TlbBlackBox extends BlackBox with HasBlackBoxResource {
  override def desiredName: String = "tlb"
  val io = FlatIO(new Bundle { /* ... */ })

  addResource("tlb.v")        // 对应 src/main/resources/tlb.v
}

The two approaches differ only in where the file lives and what the path is relative to:

Approach Where the file lives Path relative to HasBlackBoxPath + addPath anywhere in the source tree the project root HasBlackBoxResource + addResource under src/main/resources/ the resources root

Do not forget files that are included

If axi_bridge.v contains include "definition.vh", then definition.vh must be passed to addPath as well. The tool puts the files it collects into the same directory, which is how the include finds it. If you leave it out, the symptom is an undefined macro when the Verilog is compiled.

If it reports that a file cannot be found

The relative path in addPath is resolved against the project root as Chisel sees it. If it reports that the file cannot be found, specify it explicitly in the compilation options: 

-Dchisel.project.root=/你的/工程/根目录

docs.title: Beyond the BlackBox: You Still Need Glue Logic
docs.text:
A BlackBox only lines up ports; it produces no timing or protocol logic. Wiring tlb.v into the pipeline usually means writing a batch of extra logic in between:

class TlbAdapter extends Module {
  val io = IO(new Bundle {
    val req  = Flipped(Decoupled(new TlbReq))
    val resp = Decoupled(new TlbResp)
  })

  val tlb = Module(new TlbBlackBox)
  tlb.io.clk    := clock
  tlb.io.resetn := !reset.asBool

  // 请求要打拍、要排队，返回还要按顺序配回原请求 ——
  // 这些逻辑都不在 BlackBox 里，得自己写
  val reqQueue = Module(new Queue(new TlbReq, 4))
  // ...
}

The things you commonly have to add yourself:

  • Clock and reset: see the previous section;
  • Registering and queueing requests/responses: the BlackBox often takes several cycles to respond, whereas the combinational logic on the Chisel side is computed in the same cycle;
  • Protocol conversion: the Verilog side may use a pulse handshake, while the Chisel side is used to Decoupled;
  • Ports you are not using yet: connect them explicitly to 0.U / false.B — they must not be left dangling.

Verify the Verilog on its own first, then integrate it with a BlackBox

This is exactly how Labs 17 and 20 of this course are arranged: first get the Verilog module passing on its own in the module-level verification environment (module_verify/tlb_verify/, module_verify/cache_verify/) under Vivado, confirming that the port semantics are right; then, in Labs 18 and 21, integrate it into the CPU with a BlackBox.

If you integrate straight away, three classes of problem — a mistyped port name, reversed reset polarity, and a misreading of the handshake — all get mixed together and are very hard to pin down.

docs.title: Common Errors and How to Track Them Down
docs.text:
Symptom Usual cause Unknown module when compiling the Verilog desiredName does not match the module name; or the source file was never brought in with addPath / addResource "Port does not exist" at instantiation the port name in Chisel does not match Verilog (letter case, or a missing _i / _o suffix) It compiles, but the function is completely wrong a bit-width mismatch causing implicit truncation; or a direction written the wrong way round Large amounts of x in simulation the clock is not connected, the reset polarity is reversed, or an input port is left dangling Macro/parameter undefined an included header was not added; or a Map(...) parameter name does not match the Verilog parameter name

A bit-width mismatch raises no error

Declare a Verilog [31:0] as UInt(16.W) and the Verilog still compiles, but the upper bits are simply thrown away. Errors like this show up only in behavior, so you have to debug them against the waveform.

When wrapping a module with dozens of ports such as tlb.v or cache.v, copy the bit widths straight from the interface tables in Labs 17 and 20 — do not write them from memory.

docs.title: When Not to Use a BlackBox
docs.text:
The inside of a BlackBox is invisible to Chisel, and the price is:

  • No cross-module optimization — constant propagation and dead-logic elimination never reach inside the BlackBox;
  • A mistyped port name or bit width is not checked by Chisel; it surfaces only when Verilog is generated or at synthesis time;
  • The synthesis tool cannot see the internal structure, so timing is your responsibility.

So if the logic can be written clearly in Chisel, write it in Chisel. Only Verilog with a fixed interface that has already been verified is worth wrapping. This course's tlb.v and cache.v fall into that category (the lab notes require the ports to be named as defined in the book); the register file and RAM you wrote yourself in Labs 1–4 are equally good candidates if you want to reuse them from Chisel.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A BlackBox plugs an existing Verilog module into Chisel as it is: Chisel neither translates nor checks its internal logic.
  • desiredName, the port names, the port directions, the bit widths, and the parameter names must all match the Verilog exactly.
  • The clock and reset are not inserted automatically: declare them explicitly, connect them explicitly, and mind the polarity of resetn.
  • Ports are flat — use FlatIO to avoid unexpected name prefixes.
  • There are two ways to bring in the source file: HasBlackBoxPath + addPath (relative to the project root) and HasBlackBoxResource + addResource (file under src/main/resources/); included headers must be added too.
  • A BlackBox only lines up ports; queueing, protocol conversion, and constant connections are glue logic you still have to write yourself.
  • Get the Verilog passing in the module-level verification environment first, then integrate it with a BlackBox.

docs.title: Basic Syntax (Part 1): Basic Data Types
docs.text: When moving from Verilog to Chisel, the first thing to sort out is when a line of Scala runs versus when a hardware signal changes. This chapter explains those two stages first, and then introduces the data types and signals you will use most often.

docs.title: Keeping the Two Stages Apart
docs.text:
A piece of Chisel source goes through two stages.

The first is the circuit generation stage. Mill runs the Scala program; Scala's class, if, for, and functions all execute at that point, and the end result is a hardware circuit diagram.

The second is the hardware run stage. The generated SystemVerilog goes into a simulator or an FPGA, where combinational logic follows its inputs and registers update on the clock edge.

What you see When it happens What it does Scala Int, Boolean, if, for While generating the circuit Decides which circuit gets generated Chisel UInt, Bool, when, Reg While the hardware runs Represents real signals and state

A very small example:

class Adder(val width: Int) extends Module {
  val io = IO(new Bundle {
    val a = Input(UInt(width.W))
    val b = Input(UInt(width.W))
    val y = Output(UInt(width.W))
  })

  io.y := io.a + io.b
}

When you instantiate new Adder(32), the Scala parameter width is 32, and that is what decides to generate a 32-bit adder. Once generation has finished, there is no register called width in the hardware; io.a, io.b, and io.y are the signals that change at run time.

A Scala condition is not a hardware condition

The condition in if (debug) is usually a Scala Boolean: it decides whether a piece of hardware gets generated at all. The condition in when(io.enable) is a Chisel Bool, and it generates a circuit controlled by io.enable. Do not use a Scala if in place of a hardware multiplexer.

docs.title: Common Scala Syntax
docs.text: This section covers the Scala syntax you will keep coming back to when implementing a CPU; look up the rest when you need it.

docs.title: val, var, and :=
docs.text:
val means the Scala name cannot be rebound; var means it can:

val xlen = 32
var fileCount = 0
fileCount = fileCount + 1

When declaring hardware you almost always use val:

val pc = RegInit(0.U(32.W))
pc := pc + 4.U

Here pc always refers to the same hardware register, so it is a val. What val restricts is the Scala name; the bits stored in the register still change on the clock edge.

= and := also live at different levels:

Syntax Meaning val nextPC = pc + 4.U Give a hardware expression a Scala name pc := nextPC Connect the hardware expression to the register input x = y Rebind a Scala var; not a hardware assignment

Do not use var to model a register

Scala rebinding only happens during generation. To hold data across cycles in hardware, you must use Reg or RegInit.

docs.title: class, new, and object
docs.text:
class defines a structure you can create over and over. A Bundle is created with new, and a module instance additionally has to be wrapped in Module(...):

class FetchPacket extends Bundle {
  val pc = UInt(32.W)
  val inst = UInt(32.W)
}

val packet = Wire(new FetchPacket)
val alu = Module(new Alu)

object is a Scala singleton, a good place for global configuration and fixed encodings:

object CoreConfig {
  val XLEN = 32
  val RESET_PC = BigInt("80000000", 16)
}

Here XLEN and RESET_PC are both Scala constants used during generation. They do not generate any hardware of their own.

docs.title: Seq
docs.text:
Seq is a Scala sequence, roughly a read-only list. It is not hardware itself, but it can hold Chisel expressions or module instances.

val zeros = Seq.fill(32)(0.U(32.W))
val indices = Seq.tabulate(4)(i => i.U)
val adders = Seq.fill(2)(Module(new Adder(32)))

When you later meet VecInit(Seq(...)) or MuxLookup(...)(Seq(...)), the outer Seq collects a number of items during generation, and Chisel then generates a circuit from those items.

docs.title: for Loops
docs.text:
A for in Chisel is a Scala loop, and it unrolls during generation. The code below generates four copies of parallel addition logic:

for (i <- 0 until 4) {
  io.out(i) := io.in(i) + 1.U
}

It means roughly the same as writing four lines of connections by hand — not out(0) computed in cycle 0 and out(1) in cycle 1.

Distinguish it from if in software programming

A for in Chisel expresses parallelism; it is used to describe many copies of the same hardware structure.

If you need a divider that iterates over cycles, use a state machine, a counter, and registers. A Scala for only replicates or organizes hardware; it does not produce multi-cycle behavior.

yield collects the result of each iteration into a Seq:

val incremented = for (i <- 0 until 4) yield {
  io.in(i) + 1.U
}

Here incremented is a Scala sequence containing four hardware expressions.

docs.title: reduce
docs.text:
reduce merges a sequence item by item into a single result. Given a Chisel operation, it generates the corresponding combinational logic.

val sum = data.reduce(_ + _)
val anyHit = hitVec.reduce(_ || _)
val allReady = readyVec.reduce(_ && _)

_ + _ is shorthand for an anonymous function, and reads as "add the running result to the current element". For example, data.reduce(_ + _) ends up wiring every element of data into an adder network.

reduce says "merge all the elements", but it makes no promise of generating a balanced tree. When there are many inputs or the timing requirement is tight, check the generated RTL and the synthesis report.

docs.title: package and import
docs.text:
Once CPU code is split across several files, you usually put it in one namespace with package. For example, mycpu/src/cpu/Alu.scala:

package cpu

import chisel3._
import chisel3.util._

class Alu extends Module {
  // 端口与逻辑
}

Files in the cpu package can use Alu directly. To reference it across packages, write:

import cpu.Alu
import cpu.{Decoder, RegisterFile}

For a five-stage pipeline CPU at the scale of this course's labs, you do not need a fine-grained package layout. Keeping the core modules together under the cpu package is usually clear enough to start with.

docs.title: Scala Types and Chisel Types
docs.text:
The two groups of types below have similar names but different purposes:

Scala data Chisel data Difference Int, BigInt UInt, SInt The former is computed during generation; the latter represents hardware bits Boolean Bool The former controls Scala; the latter can be wired into a circuit Seq[T] Vec[T] The former is indexed by a Scala index; the latter can be selected by a hardware index

For example:

val width: Int = 32
val resetPC: BigInt = BigInt("80000000", 16)

val data = Wire(UInt(width.W))
val valid = Wire(Bool())

width and resetPC are already fixed when the circuit is generated; data and valid are the hardware signals you can see in a simulation waveform.

docs.title: Three Common Hardware Data Types
docs.text:
Chisel syntax Meaning Closest Verilog equivalent UInt(32.W) 32-bit unsigned type logic [31:0] SInt(32.W) 32-bit signed two's-complement type logic signed [31:0] Bool() Single-bit boolean type logic

These forms only describe a signal's type. It is only once you hand one to Wire, Reg, or IO that you get a hardware signal with an owner:

val aluOut = Wire(UInt(32.W))
val pc = RegInit(0.U(32.W))

You can also bind a hardware expression straight to a val, without writing an extra Wire for every intermediate result:

val nextPC = pc + 4.U
val isZero = aluOut === 0.U

nextPC and isZero still stand for hardware expressions; they simply have no separate Wire declared that could be connected more than once.

docs.title: Hardware Literals
docs.text:
Only when you add .U, .S, or .B to a Scala number does it become a Chisel hardware constant:

0.U(32.W)
"hff".U(32.W)
"b1010".U(4.W)
-3.S(8.W)
true.B
false.B

The bit width of 0.U can be inferred from where it is connected, but reset values, interface constants, masks, and addresses should normally have an explicit bit width. The next chapter continues with the result bit width of arithmetic expressions.

Always specify the bit width

Always give a literal an explicit bit width when you define it in Chisel, or you will get hard-to-diagnose errors such as bit-width problems.

docs.title: Storing Fixed Encodings in an object
docs.text:
RISC-V opcodes and ALU control codes are already fixed by the design, so it makes sense to keep them together in an object:

object AluOp {
  val ADD = 0.U(4.W)
  val SUB = 1.U(4.W)
  val AND = 2.U(4.W)
  val OR  = 3.U(4.W)
  val XOR = 4.U(4.W)
}

In use you write AluOp.ADD. Compared with 0.U and 1.U scattered all over the place, the name tells you what those bits mean.

docs.title: ChiselEnum
docs.text:
A state machine has only a handful of states, so prefer the more strongly typed ChiselEnum:

import chisel3.util.ChiselEnum

object State extends ChiselEnum {
  val IDLE, RUN, DONE = Value
}

val state = RegInit(State.IDLE)
when(state === State.IDLE) {
  state := State.RUN
}

Enumeration values have a type of their own, so if you mistakenly connect a plain UInt straight to a state signal, the compiler is much more likely to catch it for you.

docs.title: Enum(n)
docs.text:
Enum(n) is also common in older code and in shorter examples. It generates a number of plain UInt constants:

import chisel3.util.Enum

val idle :: run :: done :: Nil = Enum(3)
val state = RegInit(idle)

when(state === idle) {
  state := run
}

:: is Scala's list-decomposition syntax. The three values above correspond in order to 0.U, 1.U, and 2.U. It is fairly lightweight, but its type checking is not as strict as ChiselEnum's.

Tip

In the labs, prefer ChiselEnum for state machines; when reading existing projects, you need to recognize both forms.

docs.title: asSInt and asUInt
docs.text:
These two operations do not change the underlying bits; they only change whether those bits are interpreted as signed or unsigned:

val bits = "b1111".U(4.W)
val signed = bits.asSInt

Read as a UInt, bits is 15; read as four-bit two's complement, signed is -1. The common uses in a CPU are SLT and SRA:

val slt = a.asSInt < b.asSInt
val sra = (a.asSInt >> b(4, 0)).asUInt

Forgetting the conversion usually does not produce a syntax error; it quietly generates a different but perfectly legal circuit. So signed comparisons, negative numbers, and inputs whose top bit is 1 must all be tested separately.

Warning

Take the signed and unsigned side of things seriously, or your results will simply come out wrong!

docs.title: asTypeOf
docs.text:
asTypeOf reinterprets a group of bits according to the structure of the target type; it is very common when clearing a pipeline Bundle:

val bubble = 0.U.asTypeOf(new ID2EX)
It clears the whole structure of the target type in one step.

docs.title: Wire
docs.text:
Wire represents a signal driven by combinational logic. It does not hold its value from the previous cycle.

val result = Wire(UInt(32.W))
result := io.a + io.b

When a combinational result has a default path and a special path, you can give the default connection first and then override it:

val nextPC = WireDefault(pc + 4.U)

when(branchTaken) {
  nextPC := branchTarget
}

This generates multiplexer logic. When the condition is false the path goes through pc + 4; when it is true it goes through branchTarget.

Use DontCare with care

DontCare says that certain bits do not matter, and synthesis may optimize them away. It also makes simulation harder to read, and can even hide illegal control paths. For CPU control signals, give explicit default values first.

Explicit reset

Whether it is the Wire introduced here or the Reg registers introduced later, prefer the versions that carry a default value, so that Vivado simulation does not show X (unknown) states!

docs.title: Reg and RegInit
docs.text:
Reg and RegInit generate registers. The input is sampled on the clock edge, and the output holds between two clock edges.

val pc = RegInit("h80000000".U(32.W))
pc := pc + 4.U

RegInit specifies a reset value; Reg only specifies a type:

val valid = RegInit(false.B)
val data = Reg(UInt(32.W))

The contents of data, which has no reset value, should not be relied on after reset. The usual practice in a pipeline is to reset the valid bit of every stage and leave the data fields unreset; as long as valid is false, that data must not produce side effects such as writing a register or writing memory.

The PC, state machines, pipeline valid bits, and any state that controls external side effects should normally have an explicit reset.

Reset is mandatory for the control path and unnecessary for the data path — leaving the data path unreset avoids extra area and timing pressure.

docs.title: IO: Module Ports
docs.text:
IO declares the ports that connect a module to the outside world. The usual style is to put the ports in a Bundle:

class Alu extends Module {
  val io = IO(new Bundle {
    val a = Input(UInt(32.W))
    val b = Input(UInt(32.W))
    val out = Output(UInt(32.W))
  })

  io.out := io.a + io.b
}

Seen from inside the module, an Input can only be read, while an Output is driven by the current module. Chisel checks port directions, so trying to connect an internal result to an input port is an error.

io is the conventional name for the port variable, not something the language requires. Sticking to it makes it easier to read the interface of one module after another.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• Scala's if, for, and Int work during generation; Chisel's when, UInt, and Reg describe hardware.
  • What val fixes is the Scala name; the contents of a register can still change every cycle.
  • UInt(32.W) is a hardware type template; only once it is handed to Wire, Reg, or IO does it become a signal with an owner.
  • A Wire has no memory, so every combinational path must be fully driven; a Reg holds state across cycles.
  • = defines or rebinds a Scala name; := is what performs a hardware connection.

The next chapter builds combinational and sequential logic on top of these signals, and focuses on when, default connections, connection priority, and arithmetic bit widths.

docs.title: Basic Syntax (Part 3): Bundle, Vec and Module
docs.text: This chapter introduces Bundle, Vec and Module, which are used to organize related signals, to represent arrays of similar hardware, and to build up a module hierarchy.

docs.title: Bundle
docs.text:
Pipeline stages usually have to pass several signals along at the same time. What IF hands to ID is valid, the PC and the instruction; when ID hands over to EX there are also operands, immediates, the destination register and control signals.

If every wire is declared on its own, adding or removing a field easily leaves a connection somewhere that nobody updated. A Bundle lets you organize these signals into one unit.

docs.title: Defining Pipeline Data
docs.text:
The Bundle below represents one piece of data passed between the IF and ID stages:

class IF2ID extends Bundle {
  val valid = Bool()
  val pc = UInt(32.W)
  val inst = UInt(32.W)
}

new IF2ID only gives the field structure. You get actual hardware once you hand it to a Wire or a Reg:

val if2idNext = Wire(new IF2ID)
val if2id = RegInit(0.U.asTypeOf(new IF2ID))

Fill in the fields of the combinational version, then write the whole bundle into the pipeline register:

if2idNext.valid := fetchValid
if2idNext.pc := fetchPC
if2idNext.inst := fetchInst

when(!stall) {
  if2id := if2idNext
}

The generated RTL still has a register and the corresponding connections for each field. A Bundle changes how the code is organized; it does not reduce these hardware signals.

docs.title: Using valid to Mark a Bubble
docs.text:
When you insert a bubble, the key move is to set valid to false:

val bubble = WireDefault(0.U.asTypeOf(new IF2ID))
bubble.valid := false.B

The later connection overrides the all-zero bundle written before it. Downstream logic must guarantee that a false valid produces no side effects such as register writes or memory writes.

Writing only the instruction field as a NOP encoding does not guarantee that the other control signals are neutralized at the same time. An explicit valid lets you control stalls, flushes and external side effects in one place.

docs.title: Bundles Can Nest
docs.text:
When a group of control signals recurs in several pipeline stages, you can define a small Bundle for it:

class DecodeControl extends Bundle {
  val regWrite = Bool()
  val memRead = Bool()
  val memWrite = Bool()
  val aluOp = UInt(4.W)
}

Then put it inside the ID/EX data:

class ID2EX extends Bundle {
  val valid = Bool()
  val pc = UInt(32.W)
  val rd = UInt(5.W)
  val operandA = UInt(32.W)
  val operandB = UInt(32.W)
  val ctrl = new DecodeControl
}

Nested fields are still accessed with dots:

id2exNext.ctrl.regWrite := decoder.io.ctrl.regWrite
id2exNext.ctrl.aluOp := decoder.io.ctrl.aluOp

When the structure and the directions are compatible, you can also connect a whole bundle at once:

id2exNext.ctrl := decoder.io.ctrl

Do not nest too deeply. Control signals and datapath signals that belong to the same group can be nested; fields that are not closely related should still be organized separately.

docs.title: Vec
docs.text:
The fields of a Bundle have different names and meanings, whereas the elements of a Vec all have the same type and are accessed by index.

First, keep Seq and Vec apart:

Type What the index is When it happens Scala Seq a Scala Int one item is selected at generation time Chisel Vec can be a hardware UInt a selection circuit is generated and used at run time

modules(2) is just Scala taking item 2 of the sequence at generation time. In registers(rs1), rs1 is a hardware signal, so a read selection network controlled by the register number is generated.

docs.title: Writing a Register File with Vec
docs.text:
Here is a simple 32-entry register file:

val registers = RegInit(
  VecInit(Seq.fill(32)(0.U(32.W)))
)

val rdata1 = Mux(rs1 === 0.U, 0.U, registers(rs1))
val rdata2 = Mux(rs2 === 0.U, 0.U, registers(rs2))

The write port updates on the clock edge and protects x0:

when(writeEnable && rd =/= 0.U) {
  registers(rd) := writeData
}

docs.title: VecInit and Vec
docs.text:
VecInit builds a Vec from existing hardware elements:

val sizes = VecInit(Seq(
  1.U(3.W), 2.U(3.W), 4.U(3.W)
))

val selectedSize = sizes(sizeCode)

These common idioms can be read like this:

Form What it generates Typical use VecInit(Seq(...)) a group of combinational expressions small constant tables, decode selection Wire(Vec(n, T)) n Wires of the same type similar combinational signals Reg(Vec(n, T)) n Regs of the same type register arrays RegInit(VecInit(...)) a register array with initial values a teaching register file

docs.title: log2Ceil and log2Floor
docs.text:
Parameterized modules often need to compute an address width from the number of elements. Both log2Ceil and log2Floor are Scala functions that run at generation time; they do not generate a logarithm circuit.

import chisel3.util.{log2Ceil, log2Floor}

val ceil32 = log2Ceil(32)   // 5
val ceil31 = log2Ceil(31)   // 5
val floor32 = log2Floor(32) // 5
val floor31 = log2Floor(31) // 4

When the number of registers is a parameter, the address width usually uses log2Ceil:

class RegisterFile(val count: Int) extends Module {
  val addrWidth = log2Ceil(count)
  val io = IO(new Bundle {
    val rs1 = Input(UInt(addrWidth.W))
    val rs2 = Input(UInt(addrWidth.W))
  })
}

count is a Scala Int and is already fixed when the module is generated. You cannot pass a Chisel UInt that changes at run time to log2Ceil or log2Floor.

The count = 1 case

The mathematical result of log2Ceil(1) is 0. If a parameterized interface allows a single element, you usually need math.max(1, log2Ceil(count)) to avoid a zero-width address. A fixed 32-entry register file is not affected by this.

docs.title: Module
docs.text: Chisel's Module corresponds to Verilog's module. A module has its own ports and internal logic, and the top level connects them up by instantiating and wiring them.

docs.title: Defining an ALU Module
docs.text:
First define the control encodings in one place:

object AluOp {
  val ADD = 0.U(4.W)
  val SUB = 1.U(4.W)
  val AND = 2.U(4.W)
  val OR  = 3.U(4.W)
}

The ALU module is responsible only for computing a result from the operation code:

class Alu extends Module {
  val io = IO(new Bundle {
    val a = Input(UInt(32.W))
    val b = Input(UInt(32.W))
    val op = Input(UInt(4.W))
    val out = Output(UInt(32.W))
    val zero = Output(Bool())
  })

  val result = MuxLookup(io.op, 0.U)(Seq(
    AluOp.ADD -> (io.a + io.b),
    AluOp.SUB -> (io.a - io.b),
    AluOp.AND -> (io.a & io.b),
    AluOp.OR  -> (io.a | io.b)
  ))
  io.out := result
  io.zero := result === 0.U
}

io is a common naming convention, not a reserved keyword. The port Bundle states the directions, and inside the module you read and write the ports through io.xxx.

docs.title: Instantiation and Wiring
docs.text:
Create the ALU in the EX stage:

val alu = Module(new Alu)

alu.io.a := forwardedRs1
alu.io.b := operandB
alu.io.op := id2ex.ctrl.aluOp

val executeResult = alu.io.out

new Alu creates a Scala object, and the enclosing Module(...) tells Chisel that this is a hardware submodule instance. Leaving out Module(...) gives you the wrong hierarchy or fails outright.

Scala can also instantiate modules in bulk:

val adders = Seq.tabulate(4) { _ =>
  Module(new Adder(32))
}

This generates four adders; it does not make one adder compute four times over. Generators reduce duplicated source code, but the hardware resources are still generated per instance.

docs.title: Mem and SyncReadMem
docs.text: Before you use a memory, first establish in which cycle the read data becomes available, then choose the matching memory variant.

docs.title: Mem: Asynchronous Read
docs.text:
val mem = Mem(4096, UInt(32.W))
val readData = mem.read(readAddr)

Once the address changes, the read data changes along a combinational path. Writes still happen on the clock edge:

when(writeEnable) {
  mem.write(writeAddr, writeData)
}

docs.title: SyncReadMem: Synchronous Read
docs.text:
val mem = SyncReadMem(4096, UInt(32.W))
val readData = mem.read(readAddr, readEnable)

When readEnable is true, the address is submitted in this cycle and readData is only usable in the next cycle. The corresponding destination register number, write-back control and valid must be delayed along with it; delaying only the data by a cycle is not enough.

Property Mem SyncReadMem When read data is available in the same cycle the address changes in the cycle after the read is issued Read path combinational synchronous Always inferred as block RAM? Not necessarily Also not necessarily; it depends on how you write it and on the tool

Memory latency changes the pipeline

If your current five-stage pipeline assumes that the instruction memory and the data memory return in the same cycle, you cannot simply swap in SyncReadMem and expect the timing to line up on its own. Once the memory interface changes, the pipeline registers, the stall conditions and the control-signal alignment have to change with it.

docs.title: printf and assert
docs.text: printf and assert can go straight into a hardware module to observe or check internal state in simulation when a particular cycle is reached.

docs.title: Conditional Printing
docs.text:
when(wbValid && wbRegWrite && wbRd =/= 0.U) {
  printf(p"pc=0x${Hexadecimal(wbPC)} ")
  printf(p"x${wbRd}<-0x${Hexadecimal(wbData)}\n")
}

When debugging a pipeline, start with a write-back stage log. Each committed instruction is printed once, so the output is smaller than printing from every stage every cycle.

docs.title: Checking Properties That Must Hold
docs.text:
assert(pc(1, 0) === 0.U, "PC must be aligned")
assert(registers(0) === 0.U, "x0 must remain zero")

when(memWriteEnable) {
  assert(exmem.valid, "invalid stage wrote memory")
}

Assertions suit conditions that should never happen, such as a misaligned PC, two mutually exclusive control signals being true at the same time, or an invalid pipeline stage producing a memory write.

When debugging, first use a test to find the first failure, then print the PC, the instruction, valid and the write enables around that pipeline stage. There is no need to print every internal signal by default.

docs.title: Section Summary
docs.text:
• A Bundle organizes one piece of pipeline data by field, and valid decides whether that piece of data counts.
  • A Vec organizes similar hardware by index; indexing with a hardware signal generates a selection circuit.
  • log2Ceil and log2Floor are computed at generation time, and a register address width usually uses the former.
  • Module(new Xxx) creates a real hardware hierarchy, and instantiating in bulk from Scala replicates the hardware resources.
  • Confirm the read latency before you use a memory, and keep the control signals aligned cycle by cycle with the data.

docs.title: Basic Syntax (Part 2): Combinational and Sequential Logic
docs.text:
To tell whether a piece of Chisel is combinational or sequential, look at whether the data passes through a Reg:

  • With no Reg, the output depends only on the current inputs, so it is combinational logic.
  • Passing through a Reg, the value is saved across a clock edge, so it is sequential logic.

when and switch are only conditional-connection syntax; on their own they are not a register.

docs.title: Arithmetic and Bit Width
docs.text:
val sum  = a + b
val diff = a - b
val prod = a * b

Chisel arithmetic has definite rules for the result bit width. Take UInt addition as an example:

  • a + b and a +% b keep the width of the wider operand, and the carry out of the most significant bit is dropped.
  • a +& b is one bit wider than the wider operand, so it can keep the carry.
val a = Wire(UInt(8.W))
val b = Wire(UInt(8.W))

val wrapped = a + b   // 8 位
val full    = a +& b  // 9 位

A 32-bit addition in a CPU usually wants to wrap around naturally, so plain + is enough. When you compute a checksum or an address boundary, or when you need a carry flag, think about +&.

Check the bit width of the addition result

Two operands with different bit widths can usually be combined, and the compiler does not necessarily report an error. When you design, check that the result width is what you expect, and write tests for ALU overflow, maximum value plus one, and similar cases.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
val eq  = a === b
val neq = a =/= b
val lt  = a < b
val ge  = a >= b

Order comparisons on UInt are interpreted as unsigned, and on SInt as signed. This is how you tell RISC-V's SLT and SLTU apart:

val slt  = a.asSInt < b.asSInt
val sltu = a < b

Hardware equality and inequality use === and =/=.

Scala's == returns a Scala Boolean and is no substitute for Chisel's hardware comparison result, a Bool.

when(a === b) {
  equalCount := equalCount + 1.U
}

docs.title: Bitwise and Logical Operations
docs.text:
val andResult = a & b
val orResult  = a | b
val xorResult = a ^ b
val inverted  = ~a

Several Bool conditions are usually combined with &&, || and !:

val canWrite = wen && (rd =/= 0.U)
val mustStop = loadHazard || cacheBusy

docs.title: Shifts
docs.text:
val sll = a << shamt
val srl = a >> shamt
val sra = (a.asSInt >> shamt).asUInt

For RV32, a register shift uses only the low 5 bits of the shift amount:

val shamt = b(4, 0)

The result width of a dynamic left shift can grow with the width of the shift amount. If the ALU output must stay 32 bits wide, the 32-bit output port should constrain it; check what gets generated.

docs.title: Bit Extraction, Concatenation and Filling
docs.text:
val opcode = inst(6, 0)
val rs1    = inst(19, 15)
val sign   = inst(31)

Cat concatenates from left to right, most significant bits first:

val immS = Cat(inst(31, 25), inst(11, 7))
val addr = Cat(wordAddr, 0.U(2.W))

Fill repeats a run of bits and is often used for sign extension:

val immI = Cat(Fill(20, inst(31)), inst(31, 20))

docs.title: Mux
docs.text:
Mux(cond, whenTrue, whenFalse) corresponds to Verilog's ternary operator:

val nextPC = Mux(taken, target, pc + 4.U)

docs.title: MuxLookup
docs.text:
When the selection is driven by one encoded signal, you can use MuxLookup:

val result = MuxLookup(aluOp, 0.U(32.W))(Seq(
  AluOp.ADD -> (a + b),
  AluOp.SUB -> (a - b),
  AluOp.AND -> (a & b)
))

The first argument is the select signal and the second is the default value used when nothing matches. Both the keys and the values of the mapping entries are hardware expressions.

docs.title: MuxCase
docs.text:
MuxCase takes a list of independent conditions, and the earlier conditions win:

val fwdData = MuxCase(rsData, Seq(
  hitEx  -> exData,
  hitMem -> memData
))

This suits cases such as forwarding selection, where the priority is explicit. If the conditions are really just comparisons against the same encoded value, MuxLookup is usually clearer.

docs.title: Mux1H
docs.text:
Mux1H selects data with a set of one-hot conditions:

val result = Mux1H(Seq(
  isAdd -> (a + b),
  isSub -> (a - b),
  isAnd -> (a & b)
))

It works by masking each candidate bitwise and then OR-ing the results together. So:

  • When no condition is true, the result is usually all zeros.
  • When several conditions are true at once, the candidate values are OR-ed together bitwise, and the result is usually not what you wanted.
Need Suggested idiom Two-way select Mux Lookup on one encoded signal MuxLookup Several conditions matched in order MuxCase One-hot conditions already available Mux1H

docs.title: when Is a Conditional Connection
docs.text: when / elsewhen / otherwise can drive Wires, output ports, or Regs. What hardware gets generated depends on the target.

docs.title: Describing Combinational Logic with when
docs.text:
Give the Wire a default value first, then override it when the condition holds:

val selected = WireDefault(normalData)

when(forwardFromEx) {
  selected := exData
}.elsewhen(forwardFromMem) {
  selected := memData
}

This generates combinational selection logic with priority. The default value covers the path where no condition holds, so no connection is left undriven.

The following version is incomplete:

val selected = Wire(UInt(32.W))
when(cond) {
  selected := data
}

selected is not a register, and when cond is false it cannot "keep its old value" either. Chisel will point out during its checks that it is not driven on every path.

docs.title: Controlling Register Updates with when
docs.text:
When the assignment target is a Reg, the register keeps its value if the condition does not hold:

val pc = RegInit(0.U(32.W))

when(!stall) {
  pc := nextPC
}

This generates a register with an enable. Keeping the old value does not require writing pc := pc explicitly.

docs.title: Connection Order and Priority
docs.text:
When the same target is driven several times in one scope, the last connection written wins. The usual idiom is a default connection first, then the special cases:

pc := pc + 4.U

when(redirect) {
  pc := target
}

This reads as "normally add 4; on a redirect, jump to target". The default-plus-override structure works for both Wires and Regs.

docs.title: switch / is
docs.text:
When several branches all test different values of the same signal, switch is easier to read than a long chain of comparisons:

switch(state) {
  is(State.IDLE) { nextState := State.RUN }
  is(State.RUN)  { nextState := State.DONE }
  is(State.DONE) { nextState := State.IDLE }
}

switch is not a dedicated sequential statement either. If nextState in the example above is a Wire, it generates combinational next-state logic; if it drives the state Reg directly, it controls a register update.

A state machine is usually written as "a state register plus a next-state Wire":

val state = RegInit(State.IDLE)
val nextState = WireDefault(state)

switch(state) {
  is(State.IDLE) { when(start) { nextState := State.RUN } }
  is(State.RUN)  { when(done)  { nextState := State.DONE } }
}

state := nextState

docs.title: = vs. :=
docs.text:
The two symbols live at different levels:

Form Meaning Generates a hardware connection val x = expr Defines the Scala name x expr itself may construct hardware var x = expr Defines a Scala name that can be rebound Rebinding is not a hardware update sink := source Connects a hardware source to a hardware target Yes 
val sum = a + b
io.out := sum

The first line names a hardware expression, and the second establishes the connection from sum to the output port. There is no rule that "= is a combinational assignment and := is a sequential one".

docs.title: RegNext
docs.text:
RegNext(in) delays the input by one cycle, but carries no reset value:

val delayed = RegNext(io.in)

Use the second argument when you need a reset value:

val delayed = RegNext(io.in, 0.U)

docs.title: RegEnable
docs.text:
RegEnable samples the input only when the enable is true:

val pc = RegEnable(nextPC, 0.U(32.W), !stall)

The equivalent expanded form is:

val pc = RegInit(0.U(32.W))
when(!stall) {
  pc := nextPC
}

docs.title: Counters
docs.text:
val count = RegInit(0.U(8.W))

when(enable) {
  count := count + 1.U
}

docs.title: Default Update, Overridden in Special Cases
docs.text:
val pc = RegInit(0.U(32.W))

when(redirect) {
  pc := target
}.elsewhen(!stall) {
  pc := pc + 4.U
}

If a stall and a redirect can happen in the same cycle, you must decide explicitly which one wins. The example above tests redirect first, so the redirect wins; only when there is neither a redirect nor a stall does the PC add 4. During a stall there is no connection, so the register naturally holds its value.

docs.title: Section Summary
docs.text:
• When you see when, first check whether the assignment target is a Wire or a Reg.
  • Give a combinational Wire a default value, then override it conditionally.
  • = is a Scala definition or rebinding; := is a hardware connection.
  • Check the bit width of every addition, shift, and type conversion.

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text: In this section you will use the Mill build tool bundled with the course template to compile a Chisel module under Linux and generate SystemVerilog.

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text:
We strongly recommend doing Chisel development under WSL2 or a physical Linux machine. The instructions below use WSL2 + Ubuntu as the example.

Choosing a hardware development environment

Write your Chisel code under Linux.

docs.title: Installing WSL2 / a Linux VM / a physical Linux machine
docs.text: Look up the installation instructions for your own setup.

docs.title: Installing the Basic Tools
docs.text:
All of the commands below are run in an Ubuntu/Linux terminal. Start by updating the package index:

sudo apt update

Install the JDK, Git, and the local build tools:

sudo apt install -y openjdk-17-jdk git curl
sudo apt install -y build-essential

Then install the RTL simulation and waveform tools this course uses:

sudo apt install -y verilator gtkwave

What each of these tools does for the course is fairly simple:

Tool Role in the course JDK 17 Run Scala and Chisel Git Version control for your code g++, make Compile the C++ simulation model that Verilator generates Verilator Simulate the generated SystemVerilog GTKWave Open VCD waveform files

Check the installation with the version commands:

java -version
git --version
g++ --version
verilator --version

If all of these commands print version information, the system tools are installed. GTKWave usually opens directly on Windows 11 with WSLg; if you cannot open a graphical window inside a virtual machine, first check that the VM desktop and graphics support are working properly.

docs.title: A Minimal Chisel Project
docs.text:
For the labs we use the Chisel template provided by OSCPU, which already includes test and generation scripts and works out of the box.

  1. Clone the project 
    git clone https://github.com/OSCPU/chisel-playground.git
  2. Install Mill 
    cd chisel-playground

 curl -L https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/lihaoyi/mill-dist/1.1.8/mill-dist-1.1.8-mill.sh -o mill
 chmod +x mill
 ./mill version
    Running this downloads the dependencies automatically. When you see the version number printed, the environment is set up correctly.
  3. Test and generate Verilog 
    // 测试
make test

// 生成verilog
make verilog
    The generated Verilog files end up in the build folder.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
chisel-playground/
├── .github/workflows/     # GitHub Actions CI configuration
├── src/                   # Source code directory
│   ├── GCD.scala          # GCD module implementation
│   ├── DecoupledGCD.scala # GCD module with a Decoupled interface
│   └── Elaborate.scala    # Top-level wrapper used to generate Verilog
├── test/
│   └── src/
│       └── GCDSpec.scala  # Test code for the GCD module
├── .gitignore             # Git ignore configuration
├── .scalafmt.conf         # Scala code formatting configuration
├── Makefile               # Wraps the common Mill commands
├── build.mill             # Mill build definition file
└── README.md              # Project documentation

Tip

If you need to replace the GCD module, open src/Elaborate.scala, which is the entry point for generating Verilog. You need to replace the new GCD() in it with new MyALU() (or your own module name)! Any new Chisel files you add can simply go in the src folder.

docs.title: VS Code Development Environment
docs.text: We recommend installing the Scala(Metals), Scala Syntax (official), and Chisel syntax extensions for syntax highlighting and code completion.

docs.title: From Verilog to Chisel
docs.text:
These notes are built around the five-stage pipeline CPU, and cover only the Scala and Chisel you will use along the way.

We suggest working through them in this order:

  1. Get the environment working first, and confirm that you can generate Verilog.
  2. Learn the basic syntax, so that you can write small modules.
  3. Learn module testing and timing tests, and keep verifying as you go.
  4. Then move on to pipeline registers, forwarding, stalling, and flushing.

The examples that follow are set side by side with Verilog wherever possible.

docs.title: What Chisel Is
docs.text:
Chisel stands for Constructing Hardware in a Scala Embedded Language. It is a hardware construction library built on top of Scala, not a separate language unrelated to Scala.

The Chisel code you write first runs as a Scala program and constructs a circuit; the toolchain then generates Verilog or SystemVerilog from it. The result can still be handed to Verilator for RTL simulation, or to Vivado for simulation, synthesis, and implementation on an FPGA.

Scala / Chisel source
        ↓
Run Scala, construct the circuit
        ↓
Generate Verilog / SystemVerilog
        ↓
Simulation, synthesis, running on the board

Two layers need to be kept apart here:

  • Scala syntax such as for, if, classes, and functions usually executes while the circuit is being generated.
  • Chisel constructs such as Mux, when, Reg, and := describe the hardware that gets generated.

Mix the two stages up and your code may well compile, yet still generate a different circuit from the one you intended. The syntax chapters that follow return to this point.

docs.title: Why Use Chisel
docs.text:
A single-cycle CPU is small enough that wiring everything by hand is usually manageable. With a pipelined CPU, the problems grow quickly:

  • Every pipeline register has to carry a batch of data and control signals.
  • Adding one control signal often means editing several modules and inter-stage registers at the same time.
  • Forwarding, stalling, and flushing make the top-level wiring complicated fast.
  • Parameters such as bit width, number of stages, and queue depth tend to get scattered all over the code.

Tip

Chisel will not solve pipeline hazards for you, and it cannot guarantee that your microarchitecture is correct. What it mainly does is generate repeated structures, organize related signals, and catch some connection and type problems at generation time.

docs.title: A Few Comparisons First
docs.text: You are not expected to follow the code below yet; just get a feel for how concise Chisel is.

docs.title: Multiplexer
docs.text:
Verilog usually reaches for case:

always @(*) begin
    case (sel)
        2'd0: out = a;
        2'd1: out = b;
        2'd2: out = c;
        default: out = d;
    endcase
end

Chisel can write the selection as a table:

val out = MuxLookup(sel, d)(Seq(
  0.U -> a,
  1.U -> b,
  2.U -> c
))

Both snippets generate combinational selection logic. MuxLookup is not a software table lookup, and it does not search item by item at run time.

docs.title: Register File
docs.text:
Chisel's Vec can be indexed by a hardware signal, which makes it a good fit for describing a small register array:

val regs = RegInit(VecInit(Seq.fill(32)(0.U(32.W))))

val rdata1 = Mux(rs1 === 0.U, 0.U, regs(rs1))
val rdata2 = Mux(rs2 === 0.U, 0.U, regs(rs2))

The write port is still sequential logic:

when(wen && rd =/= 0.U) {
  regs(rd) := wdata
}

Here when is not a "sequential statement". A register write is generated because the assignment target regs(rd) comes from a Reg. The same when can also drive a Wire, and then it generates combinational logic.

docs.title: Passing Signals as a Group
docs.text:
Between pipeline stages you often need to carry the PC, the instruction, and a valid bit along together. Put them in a Bundle first:

class IfId extends Bundle {
  val valid = Bool()
  val pc    = UInt(32.W)
  val inst  = UInt(32.W)
}

Then save the whole group in a single register:

val ifId = RegInit(0.U.asTypeOf(new IfId))
val ifIdNext = WireDefault(ifId)

ifId := ifIdNext
