To add a field, add it to the Bundle definition. The logic that produces this group of signals still needs the corresponding connection, and the compiler will flag any field you leave undriven.

docs.title: Design Problems You Still Have to Solve Yourself
docs.text:
Beginners tend to mistake "short code" for "simple hardware", but the two are not the same thing: short Chisel code still generates the same hardware structure.

  • One line of multiplication still generates a multiplier.
  • A Vec indexed by a hardware signal can still generate a very large multiplexer.
  • A long combinational expression can still become a critical path.
  • A for loop unrolls into hardware; it does not make one copy of that hardware automatically reused over several cycles.

Tip

When you write Chisel you still have to care about bit width, timing, parallelism, and resources. Chisel mainly changes how the code is organized and generated; it does not change these hardware constraints.

Warning

Always keep in mind that different ways of writing Chisel generate different hardware structures!!!

The next section sets up the environment and generates your first SystemVerilog file.

docs.title: Advanced Features
docs.text: This section is not a prerequisite for the basic five-stage pipeline. On a first reading you can just get to know Decoupled; the rest can be consulted once the CPU's basic functionality is working.

docs.title: The Decoupled Handshake
docs.text:
In a pipelined CPU, data cannot move between adjacent stages every single cycle.

A load-use hazard needs a stall and a jump needs a flush; the cache and the bus may also have unpredictable latency. The Chisel standard library uses DecoupledIO as a uniform way to express the ready/valid handshake, but the protocol will not handle branch flushing or pipeline state for you.

In the pipeline example above, stalls and flushes are controlled by conditional connections on the stage registers. When you connect modules that have wait states, such as the I-Cache or the data bus, you also need a uniform way to say "is this request valid" and "can the other end accept it". DecoupledIO provides that set of handshake signals.

docs.title: The Three Parts of DecoupledIO
docs.text:
// DecoupledIO 的简化定义（在 chisel3.util 中）
class DecoupledIO[T <: Data](gen: T) extends Bundle {
    val ready = Input(Bool())    // 接收方说"我可以收了"
    val valid = Output(Bool())   // 发送方说"我有数据要传"
    val bits  = Output(gen)      // 实际数据（类型为泛型 T）
}

A successful transfer happens on the clock edge where ready && valid are both true — what is usually called fire.

Once the producer raises valid, it should hold valid and bits steady until the transfer completes. Otherwise, if the consumer applies backpressure, the data being waited on may change.

Decoupled defines only the interface protocol

DecoupledIO provides ready, valid, bits, and a few related helper methods. Whether the producer really holds its data steady, whether the queue is deep enough, and how requests on an error path are canceled are still up to you as the designer.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
// 生产者：声明 Decoupled 输出端口
class Producer extends Module {
    val io = IO(new Bundle {
        val out = Decoupled(UInt(32.W))
    })
    val dataReg = RegInit(0.U(32.W))

    io.out.bits  := dataReg
    io.out.valid := true.B

    when(io.out.fire) { dataReg := dataReg + 1.U }
}

// 消费者：声明 Decoupled 输入端口
class Consumer extends Module {
    val io = IO(new Bundle {
        val in     = Flipped(Decoupled(UInt(32.W)))
        val enable = Input(Bool())
    })
    val dataReg = RegInit(0.U(32.W))
    io.in.ready := io.enable

    when(io.in.fire) {
        dataReg := io.in.bits
    }
}

What Flipped does: Decoupled defaults to the "output" orientation (ready as an input, valid/bits as outputs).

A consumer needs the opposite: ready as an output and valid/bits as inputs. Flipped flips the whole orientation in one go, with no need to rewrite the Input/Output of all three fields by hand.

docs.title: fire()
docs.text:
DecoupledIO provides several convenience methods; fire among them means that ready and valid are both high, that is, the transfer succeeded:

io.out.ready
io.out.valid
io.out.bits
io.out.fire   // 等价于 io.out.ready && io.out.valid

The common pattern on the producer side:

// 典型的 Decoupled 生产者：fire 后更新下一笔数据
when(io.out.fire) {
    // 上一笔数据已被接收，准备下一笔
    dataReg := nextData
}

A data source of finite length can add a validReg; you lower it once the last item has been sent.

docs.title: Bulk Connection with <>
docs.text:
Chisel provides the <> operator for connecting two Bundles of the same structure in bulk:

producer.io.out <> consumer.io.in
// 等价于：
// consumer.io.in.ready -> producer.io.out.ready
// producer.io.out.valid -> consumer.io.in.valid
// producer.io.out.bits  -> consumer.io.in.bits

<> matches fields by name and connects them according to their Input/Output directions. Interfaces whose structure and directions are compatible can be connected as a whole, with no need to write := field by field.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
Queue inserts a FIFO between producer and consumer and propagates backpressure:

val producer = Module(new Producer)
val consumer = Module(new Consumer)

consumer.io.in <> Queue(producer.io.out, 2)

When you need other behavior, switch to the parameterized version rather than keeping the connection above as well:

consumer.io.in <> Queue(
    producer.io.out,
    entries = 4,        // FIFO 深度
    pipe    = true,
    flow    = false
)

The basic behavior is as follows:

  • when the consumer's ready=0, data is buffered in the queue
  • when the queue is full, the producer sees ready=0 and pauses automatically
  • when the queue is empty, the consumer sees valid=0 and knows there is no data available

flow = true lets the input pass combinationally straight through to the output when the queue is empty; pipe = true lets an enqueue proceed when the queue is full but an item is dequeued in the same cycle. Both change the combinational path of ready/valid, so neither should be thought of simply as an extra pipeline register. Whether they improve timing depends on the particular connection and on the synthesis result.

docs.title: Pipe
docs.text:
Pipe works on ValidIO: it delays only valid and bits, and has no ready and no backpressure:

val staged1 = Pipe(io.in)
val staged3 = Pipe(io.in, latency = 3)

It suits a delay path where the consumer can accept data every cycle. If the downstream side may pause, use DecoupledIO with Queue — Pipe is not a substitute.

Choosing between a plain Bundle and Decoupled

Situation What to use Why Between pipeline stages (there are stalls/flushes, and the control logic must be exact for every cycle) a plain Bundle + manual when control hold, clear, and normal update are described separately Fetch ↔ I-Cache, memory access ↔ bus DecoupledIO the request may have to wait, so a ready/valid handshake is needed Between two modules with mismatched rates DecoupledIO + Queue the Queue buffers data the downstream side has not accepted yet One-way push, no backpressure needed (e.g. interrupt signals, branch prediction results) ValidIO (see the next section) the interface contains no ready

For the basic five-stage pipeline, use plain Bundles for the inter-stage registers and handle stall/flush manually. Reach for Decoupled when connecting modules that may wait, such as the cache or the bus.

docs.title: Other Common Construction Primitives
docs.text: Besides Mux, RegInit, and Bundle, chisel3.util offers other everyday components such as ValidIO, Counter, ShiftRegister, and Arbiter. Their interfaces and the conditions under which they apply are described below.

docs.title: ValidIO
docs.text:
ValidIO has only valid and bits, no ready. It suits one-way paths where the consumer can always accept data and no backpressure is needed.

// ValidIO 的定义（在 chisel3.util 中）
class ValidIO[T <: Data](gen: T) extends Bundle {
    val valid = Output(Bool())
    val bits  = Output(gen)
}

// 生产者：声明 Valid 输出
class BranchPredictor extends Module {
    val io = IO(new Bundle {
        val prediction = Valid(UInt(32.W))   // 预测的目标地址 + 是否有效
    })
    io.prediction.bits  := predictedTarget
    io.prediction.valid := hasPrediction     // 没有预测时 valid=0，bits 值无效
}

// 消费者：取指单元检查 valid 决定是否跳转
val pc_next = Mux(predictor.io.prediction.valid,
                  predictor.io.prediction.bits,
                  pc + 4.U)
Situation What to use Reason The consumer may be unable to accept, so backpressure is needed DecoupledIO the consumer can hold off the transfer via ready The consumer can always accept, and only data and a valid flag are passed ValidIO the interface contains no ready

docs.title: Counter
docs.text:
Counter implements a counter and packages up the common pattern of counting conditionally and wrapping around when the limit is reached:

// Counter(cond, n)：cond 为 true 时计数 +1，计到 n-1 后下一个周期回 0
val (count, wrap) = Counter(true.B, 32)        // 每周期 +1，0→31→0→31→...
val (count, wrap) = Counter(en, 100)           // 有条件计数

// count: UInt —— 当前计数值（0 到 n-1）
// wrap:  Bool —— 当 count === n-1 且 cond 为 true 时为真

Iteration counting in a multi-cycle divider:

val (cycle, done) = Counter(state === RUN, 32)  // RUN 状态每周期 +1

when(state === RUN) {
    // 迭代除法算法的每一步
    remainder := remainder - divisor
    // ...
    when(done) { state := DONE }   // 32 个周期后完成
}

Compare with the hand-written version:

// 手写版本容易忘记 wrap 条件判断的细节
val cycle = RegInit(0.U(5.W))
when(state === RUN) {
    cycle := cycle + 1.U
}
val done = cycle === 31.U && state === RUN

// Counter 版本意图更清晰，且自动处理位宽
val (cycle, done) = Counter(state === RUN, 32)

Counter infers the bit width for you

In Counter(cond, n), n is a Scala Int, and count takes the bit width log2Ceil(n), enough to represent 0 to n-1.

docs.title: ShiftRegister
docs.text:
ShiftRegister gives you a multi-cycle delay: it is equivalent to several RegNexts chained together, plus an optional enable signal:

// ShiftRegister(in, n)：将 in 延迟 n 拍
val delayed = ShiftRegister(io.in, 3)
// 等价于：
// val delayed = RegNext(RegNext(RegNext(io.in)))

// ShiftRegister(in, n, en)：带使能的版本——en=1 时移位，en=0 时保持
val delayed = ShiftRegister(io.in, 3, en)
// 等价于 3 个带使能的 RegEnable 串联

// ShiftRegister(in, n, resetData, en)：额外指定复位值
val delayed = ShiftRegister(io.in, 3, 0.U, en)

A typical case in the CPU — keeping a control signal aligned with data that has been delayed:

// EX 阶段计算出的 aluResult 经过 MEM→WB 两级才写回
// regWrite 标志也需要打同样的拍数，保持与数据同步
val regWrite_mem = RegNext(regWrite_ex)
val regWrite_wb  = RegNext(regWrite_mem)

// 用 ShiftRegister 一行搞定
val regWrite_delayed = ShiftRegister(regWrite_ex, 2)   // 打 2 拍，对齐到 WB

docs.title: Arbiter: the Many-to-One Scheduler
docs.text:
When several requesters compete for the same resource (two masters sharing a bus, say), the arbiter decides between them. chisel3.util provides two ready-made arbiters:

val arb = Module(new Arbiter(UInt(32.W), 4))
arb.io.in(0) <> req0
arb.io.in(1) <> req1
arb.io.in(2) <> req2
arb.io.in(3) <> req3
arb.io.out <> sharedBus

The round-robin arbiter has the same interface:

val rrArb = Module(new RRArbiter(UInt(32.W), 4))

Distinguishing Arbiter from RRArbiter

Arbiter is a fixed-priority arbiter: when several inputs are valid at once it picks the lower-numbered one. RRArbiter uses a round-robin policy.

Both have DecoupledIO on their inputs and on their output. A transfer completes when the selected requester has valid=1 and the output has ready=1; the round-robin arbiter then moves its starting point, while the fixed-priority arbiter still begins from the lowest-numbered valid request.

Arbitration in a CPU

A single-core teaching CPU will not necessarily need an Arbiter. When the I-Cache and D-Cache have to share one external bus interface, an arbiter can be used to select the current request.

docs.title: PriorityMux and PriorityEncoder
docs.text:
PriorityEncoder returns the index of the highest-priority set bit, which by default means low bits first. PriorityMux selects the first value in a list whose condition holds.

val irq = Wire(UInt(8.W))

// irq(0) 优先级最高，其次是 irq(1)
val irqNum = PriorityEncoder(irq)

When irq is all zeros the encoded result is also zero, so you must check irq.orR separately to tell whether there really is a request.

// PriorityMux: 按优先级选择——第一个满足条件的值被选中
val result = PriorityMux(Seq(
    (cond0) -> value0,    // 优先级最高——cond0 先被检查
    (cond1) -> value1,
    (cond2) -> value2     // 优先级最低
))

PriorityMux, MuxCase, and Mux1H

PriorityMux and MuxCase both express an ordered priority selection and do not require the conditions to be mutually exclusive. Only Mux1H assumes the select conditions are one-hot; if several are true at once, it ORs the candidate data together bit by bit.

docs.title: Parameterization and Code Generation
docs.text: Scala's constructor parameters, collections, and functions can be used to generate configurable hardware structures. Here are three patterns that come up often in this course's project.

docs.title: Generic Modules
docs.text:
Put parameters such as bit width, depth, and count in the class constructor, and passing different values at instantiation gives you modules of different sizes:

// 参数化 ALU：位宽可变
class Alu(width: Int) extends Module {
    val io = IO(new Bundle {
        val a   = Input(UInt(width.W))
        val b   = Input(UInt(width.W))
        val op  = Input(UInt(4.W))
        val out = Output(UInt(width.W))
    })
    io.out := MuxLookup(io.op, 0.U(width.W))(Seq(
        AluOp.ADD -> (io.a + io.b),
        AluOp.SUB -> (io.a - io.b),
        // ...
    ))
}

// 实例化 32 位和 64 位两种 ALU
val alu32 = Module(new Alu(32))
val alu64 = Module(new Alu(64))
// 两个实例使用相同结构，位宽参数不同

// 参数化寄存器堆：寄存器数量和位宽都可配置
class RegFile(regCount: Int, xlen: Int) extends Module {
    val addrWidth = log2Ceil(regCount)
    val io = IO(new Bundle {
        val rs1 = Input(UInt(addrWidth.W))     // 地址位宽自动匹配寄存器数量
        val rs2 = Input(UInt(addrWidth.W))
        val rd  = Input(UInt(addrWidth.W))
        val wen = Input(Bool())
        val wdata = Input(UInt(xlen.W))
        val rdata1 = Output(UInt(xlen.W))
        val rdata2 = Output(UInt(xlen.W))
    })
    val rf = RegInit(VecInit(Seq.fill(regCount)(0.U(xlen.W))))
    io.rdata1 := Mux(io.rs1 === 0.U, 0.U, rf(io.rs1))
    io.rdata2 := Mux(io.rs2 === 0.U, 0.U, rf(io.rs2))
    when(io.wen && io.rd =/= 0.U) {
        rf(io.rd) := io.wdata
    }
}

RV32 and RV64 both have 32 general-purpose integer registers; the difference is the data width:

val rf32 = Module(new RegFile(32, 32))
val rf64 = Module(new RegFile(32, 64))

Scala code runs at generation time

Constructor parameters, log2Ceil, and Seq.fill are all Scala. if, for, and functions can decide the number of modules, the bit widths, and the wiring structure at generation time, but they never become control flow in the running hardware.

docs.title: Writing a Decode Table with BitPat
docs.text:
Use the ? of BitPat for the "don't care" bits of instruction decoding, not the hardware value DontCare. The example below assumes InstType and AluOp are encoded as UInt; ListLookup can look up several control signals in one go:

val default = List(InstType.ILLEGAL, AluOp.NOP, 0.U(1.W))

val table = Array(
  BitPat("b0000000??????????000?????0110011") ->
    List(InstType.ADD, AluOp.ADD, 1.U(1.W)),
  BitPat("b0100000??????????000?????0110011") ->
    List(InstType.SUB, AluOp.SUB, 1.U(1.W))
)

After the lookup, give each result a name:

val decoded = ListLookup(io.inst, default, table)

val instType = decoded(0)
val aluOp    = decoded(1)
val regWrite = decoded(2).asBool

A table like this puts instruction bit patterns and control signals side by side. When you add an instruction you still have to add tests, and in particular you should check whether two BitPats could ever match at the same time.

docs.title: for / yield
docs.text:
When the number of a module's ports or submodules is decided by a parameter, for / yield is the standard tool:

val banks = Seq.fill(numBanks)(Module(new CacheBank(bankSize)))

banks.zipWithIndex.foreach { case (bank, i) =>
  bank.io.addr  := io.addr
  bank.io.wdata := io.wdata
  bank.io.wen   := io.wen && (bankSel === i.U)
}

If the hit signals of the banks are guaranteed to be one-hot, you can select the read data directly:

val choices = banks.map(bank => bank.io.hit -> bank.io.rdata)
io.rdata := Mux1H(choices)

// 流水线延迟线：N 级参数化
class DelayLine[T <: Data](gen: T, stages: Int) extends Module {
    val io = IO(new Bundle {
        val in  = Input(gen)
        val out = Output(gen)
    })
    io.out := (0 until stages).foldLeft(io.in) { (sig, _) =>
        RegNext(sig)   // 每一级打一拍，共 stages 拍
    }
}

// 使用：生成一个 5 级延迟线
val delay = Module(new DelayLine(UInt(32.W), 5))

Generating a cascade with foldLeft

foldLeft is a higher-order function on Scala collections: it combines an initial value with each element of the collection in turn:

// foldLeft 展开过程（以 stages=3 为例）
(0 until 3).foldLeft(io.in) { (sig, _) => RegNext(sig) }
// = RegNext(RegNext(RegNext(io.in)))

foldLeft is well suited to generating repeated structures that chain one stage onto the next, such as delay lines or bypass selection chains. It folds in order and will not restructure the operation into a balanced tree.

Counter, Queue, and parameterized modules can be used where the situation calls for them. Once the timing and behavior of your basic CPU are confirmed, use these components to tidy up repeated structure.

docs.title: Digital Logic Fundamentals
docs.text:
For every lab from here on, read the explanatory part of the corresponding chapter of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition first, then come back to these notes for the lab requirements and complete them.

Warning

The lab notes on this site are the authoritative statement of all lab requirements. Do not follow the lab requirements given in CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition!

Reference in the Book

The labs in this section correspond to Chapter 3, Fundamentals of Digital Logic Circuit Design of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, and they form the foundation for every CPU lab that follows.

Before you start designing a CPU, you need to be fluent in writing, simulating and programming three kinds of basic building block: the register file, RAM, and a complete small digital logic system.

The three practical tasks in this section take you through that process.

docs.title: Lab List
docs.text: Lab Topic Reference in the Book Lab 1: Running Light Simulate and program the running light 2.3.2 Practical Task 1 Lab 2: Register File Simulation Write and simulate the register file, a core CPU component 3.1.1 Practical Task 2 Lab 3: Synchronous and Asynchronous RAM Understand how the two RAM styles differ in timing, and complete simulation, synthesis and implementation 3.1.2 Practical Task 3 Lab 4: Digital Logic Design and Debugging Complete a small system end to end on your own: design, simulation and board debugging 3.1.3 Practical Task 4

docs.title: Lab 1: Running Light
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 2.3.2 Practical Task 1: Running Light

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Get comfortable with the Vivado workflow: creating a project, running a simulation, and programming the board.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
The lab environment is in the dc_env/exp1/ directory, with the following structure: 

|--scroller.v    Source file for the running light design
|--scroller.xdc  Constraints file for the running light design
|--testbench.v   Simulation file for the running light design

Using the three files provided — scroller.v (the design), scroller.xdc (the constraints) and testbench.v (the testbench) — build a Vivado project, then simulate and program the running light design.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
You do not need to modify any code!!!

  1. Create a new project in Vivado.
  2. Click "Add Sources" and add the design source (scroller.v).
  3. Click "Add Sources", choose simulation sources, and add testbench.v.
  4. Run the simulation, and observe the LED signal in the waveform viewer.
  5. Program the board.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text: • The running light effect is visible on the board.

docs.title: Lab 2: Register File Simulation
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 3.1.1 Practical Task 2: Register File Simulation

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the role the register file plays in a CPU: the place where operands are held.
  • Learn how to verify read/write timing by simulation, and how to read a waveform to confirm behavior.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
The lab environment is in the dc_env/exp2/ directory, with the following structure: 

|--regfile.v             Register file source file.
|--rf_tb.v               Register file simulation file.

Simulate a register file design functionally, and learn how it behaves by examining the simulation waveform.

The register file source provided in the environment has a "two-read, one-write" structure: two read ports (with no enable control, so they are permanently enabled) and one write port.

docs.title: Interface Signals
docs.text: Signal Direction Width Description clk Input 1 Clock we Input 1 Register file write enable waddr Input 5 Register file write address wdata Input 32 Register file write data raddr1 Input 5 Register file read address 1 rdata1 Output 32 Register file read data 1 raddr2 Input 5 Register file read address 2 rdata2 Output 32 Register file read data 2

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Create a new project in Vivado.
  2. Click "Add Sources", choose design sources, and add regfile.v.
  3. Click "Add Sources", choose simulation sources, and add rf_tb.v.
  4. Run the simulation, and observe the register file's read and write behavior in the waveform viewer.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text: • Run the simulation, and observe the register file's read and write behavior in the waveform viewer.

docs.title: Lab 3: Synchronous and Asynchronous RAM
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 3.1.2 Practical Task 3: Simulation, Synthesis and Implementation of Synchronous and Asynchronous RAM

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Instantiate a synchronous RAM from the Xilinx IP library, simulate it to observe how it behaves, then synthesize and implement it and inspect the timing results and resource utilization.
  • Instantiate an asynchronous RAM from the Xilinx IP library, simulate it to observe how it behaves, then synthesize and implement it and inspect the timing results and resource utilization.
  • Compare and analyze what you observe.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Both instruction fetch and memory access need RAM. FPGAs offer two common styles of RAM:

Property Asynchronous RAM Synchronous RAM Read data output Driven combinationally as soon as the address is valid The address is sampled on a clock edge, and the data appears at the next edge (or one cycle later) FPGA resource it maps to Synthesized into distributed RAM (LUTs) Can be mapped onto Block RAM (BRAM) Timing Poor timing at large capacities Good timing; suits large, high-frequency designs

The key difference is in the read timing: with an asynchronous RAM the read data appears in the same cycle as the address, whereas with a synchronous RAM the read address is registered first and the data appears one cycle later.

After synthesis and implementation, compare how much LUT and BRAM each design uses in Vivado's resource report, and you will see directly how the synthesizer maps different coding styles onto different hardware resources.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
The lab environment is in the dc_env/exp3/ directory, with the following structure: 

|--block_ram_top.v       Top-level source file for the synchronous RAM (Block RAM).
|--distributed_ram_top.v Top-level source file for the asynchronous RAM (Distributed RAM).
|--ram.xdc               Constraints file for both RAMs, used for synthesis and implementation.
|--ram_tb.v              Simulation file for both RAMs, used for simulation.

The top-level design files provided in the environment wrap the two RAM styles so that they share the same module name and interface. The top-level interface of the wrapped RAM is as follows.

docs.title: Module Interface (identical for both RAM styles)
docs.text:
Signal Direction Width Description clk Input 1 Clock ram_wen Input 1 RAM write enable: 1 selects a write, 0 selects a read ram_addr Input 10 RAM address; this signal gives both the read and the write address ram_wdata Input 32 Data written to the RAM ram_rdata Output 32 Data read out of the RAM

Note: the wrapped RAM interface has no chip-select signal, so the chip select is always active (the chip-select enable of the actual RAM instantiated inside it is tied to 1).

docs.title: Create the synchronous RAM project
docs.text:
1. Create a new project in Vivado.
  2. Click "Add Sources", choose design sources, and add block_ram_top.v.
  3. Click "Add Sources", choose constraints, and add ram.xdc.
  4. Click "Add Sources", choose simulation sources, and add ram_tb.v.
  5. Use the Xilinx IP library to generate a synchronous RAM (Block RAM, depth 65536, width 32, with the chip-select enable tied permanently active).

Customizing the synchronous RAM IP core

If you are not sure how to generate the synchronous RAM IP core, see: Customizing a synchronous RAM IP core

docs.title: Create the asynchronous RAM project
docs.text:
1. Create a new project in Vivado.
  2. Click "Add Sources", choose design sources, and add distributed_ram_top.v.
  3. Click "Add Sources", choose constraints, and add ram.xdc.
  4. Click "Add Sources", choose simulation sources, and add ram_tb.v.
  5. Use the Xilinx IP library to generate an asynchronous RAM (Distributed RAM, depth 65536, width 32

Customizing the asynchronous RAM IP core

If you are not sure how to generate the asynchronous RAM IP core, see: Customizing an asynchronous RAM IP core

Once both projects are set up, simulate them and compare how their read and write behavior differs. After the simulations, synthesize and implement both, inspect the timing results and resource utilization, and analyze them together with the read/write timing.

Viewing the timing results and resource utilization

To view the timing results and resource utilization, see: Viewing the timing results and resource utilization

While working through this lab, pay particular attention to the following points:

  • When you generate the IP, name it block_ram or distributed_ram as appropriate. A wrong name will make the IP report an error. If you find that an IP you have already generated cannot be renamed, delete it and generate it again.
  • While generating the IP you can click the diagram on the left of the window to inspect the interface. When the parameters are correct, the port names and widths should match the instantiation in the top-level file.
  • If you are interested, research the documentation on customizing synchronous and asynchronous RAM yourself, and use the simulation waveforms to compare what the parameters do.
  • Before synthesizing, make sure the constraints file (ram.xdc) has been loaded correctly.
  • When adding the testbench, be sure to choose "Add Simulation Source"; otherwise the top level will be wrong and the synthesis results will be incorrect.
  • Synthesis time depends on the machine you use and can be considerable, so plan ahead and allow enough time.
  • The timing report and the resource report are only meaningful once synthesis and implementation have finished.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• Simulate both RAM styles and observe their read/write timing in the waveform
  • Compare the timing results and resource utilization of the synchronous and asynchronous RAM

docs.title: Lab 4: Digital Logic Design and Debugging
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 3.1.3 Practical Task 4: Design and Debugging of Digital Logic Circuits

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Complete the whole flow of a full digital system on your own: "design → simulate → synthesize → program → debug".
  • Learn the basic techniques for debugging on the board.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
The lab environment is in the dc_env/exp4/ directory, with the following structure: 

|--show_sw.v             Source file for the digital circuit design.
|--show_sw.xdc           Constraints file for the design, used for synthesis and implementation.
|--tb.v                  Simulation file for the design, used for simulation.
The design in show_sw.v contains five bugs. Its correct behavior is:

  1. Read the state of the four rightmost DIP switches on the board (taken as "up = 1, down = 0"; on the actual board, a switch that is up is low and one that is down is high), giving 16 states (numbered 0~15).
  2. The leftmost seven-segment display shows the state of the four DIP switches in real time. The display can only show 0~9, so if the switch state is 10~15 the display does not change (it keeps showing the previous value).
  3. The four rightmost single-color LEDs show the previous state of the DIP switches, covering 0~15 (a switch that is up means the corresponding LED is lit).

For example: in the initial state, with all four DIP switches down, press reset and the display shows 0 with all LEDs off; set the DIP switches to 1 and the display shows 1, with the LEDs still all off; set the DIP switches to 3 and the display shows 3 while the LEDs show 1.

The design source provided contains five bugs. Four of them produce the first four kinds of waveform anomaly: the waveform being "Z", the waveform being "X", the waveform stopping, and sampling across a clock edge; the fifth bug is a functional bug.

The top-level interface of the example design provided for this task is as follows:

Name Width Direction Description clk 1 input Clock signal resetn 1 input Reset signal switch 4 input Corresponds to the four rightmost DIP switches on the board num_csn 8 output Chip-select signals for the seven-segment display num_a_g 7 output Seven-segment signals for the seven-segment display led 4 output Corresponds to the four rightmost single-color LEDs on the board

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Create a new project in Vivado.
  2. Click "Add Sources", choose design sources, and add show_sw.v.
  3. Click "Add Sources", choose constraints, and add show_sw.xdc.
  4. Click "Add Sources", choose simulation sources, and add tb.v.
  5. Work out what the example design is supposed to do, examine the simulation top level tb.v, and understand what the simulation does.
  6. Run the simulation, and make good use of the waveform viewer's aids (splitting, grouping, color changes, markers and so on) to debug it and find all the bugs.
  7. Once the simulation is correct, synthesize and implement the design and generate the bitstream.
  8. After the bitstream has been generated, connect the board and verify the design on hardware.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• In simulation the LED value is 0, 7, 6, 1, d, f in that order.
  • The behavior described above is reproduced correctly on the board.

docs.title: Single-Cycle CPU Design
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

The labs in this section correspond to Chapter 4, Single-Cycle CPU Design of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition.

A single-cycle CPU is your first complete processor: every instruction carries out instruction fetch, decode, execute, memory access, and write back within one clock cycle.

This section starts from the smallest possible system of 5 instructions, then extends it to 20 instructions and builds an automated debugging framework based on trace comparison.

Development Language

As the course schedule specifies, the single-cycle CPU is developed in Verilog, while the pipelined CPU and everything after it use Chisel. The examples in the book are mostly Verilog, so you can follow along directly.

Understanding the Design Approach

Whether you develop in Verilog or in Chisel, the early CPU design work cannot be skipped! You must get the CPU's architecture and operating principles clear; if it feels hard, sketch the module diagram by hand and draw out the execution path of a few common instructions.

docs.title: Lab List
docs.text: Lab Topic Reference in the Book Lab 5: Single-Cycle CPU with Five Instructions Build a single-cycle CPU that can run a program with the smallest possible instruction set 4.1 / 4.3.1 Lab 6: Single-Cycle CPU with Twenty Instructions Extend the instruction set and bring in the trace-comparison debugging framework and functional tests 4.2 / 4.3.2

docs.title: Lab 5: Single-Cycle CPU with Five Instructions
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition 4.1 Verifying a Single-Cycle CPU with 5 Instructions / 4.3.1 Practical Task 5

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the datapath of a single-cycle CPU: instruction fetch → decode → execute → memory access → write back, all completed within one cycle.
  • Become familiar with the organization and workflow of the lab environment (minicpu_env).
  • Be able to simulate and run on the board a single-cycle CPU supporting 5 instructions, and to run a simple test program.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The directory structure of the whole minicpu_env lab environment, together with a brief description of what each part does, is shown below: 

|--miniCPU/             RTL code of the CPU you implement
|  |--minicpu_top.v     Top-level module of the 5-instruction single-cycle CPU
|  |--regfile.v         Register file module in the CPU
|  |--tools.v           Basic functional modules in the CPU
|
|--func/                Functional verification test programs
|  |--inst_ram.coe      Binary pure-data file of the test program, used when running on the board
|  |--inst_ram.mif      Binary pure-data file of the test program, used for functional simulation
|  |--inst_ram.txt      Assembly code description of the test program
|
|--soc_verify/          Verification environment for the CPU you implement
   |--rtl/              Directory of the SoC design code used for verification
   |  |--soc_mini_top.v Top-level file of the SoC
   |  |--CONFREG/       The confreg module, used to access board peripherals such as the LEDs and the DIP switches
   |  |--xilinx_ip/     Customized Xilinx IP, including clk_pll and inst_ram
   |
   |--testbench/        Functional simulation verification platform
   |
   |--run_vivado/       The run directory of the Vivado project
      |--constraints/   Design constraints for the Vivado project
From this point on, you do not need to create the Vivado project by hand — we provide a script in the lab environment that creates it for you! The soc_verify/run_vivado/create_project.tcl script creates the Vivado project in one step!

1.Open Vivado, and in the Tcl Console at the bottom first enter the miniCPU/soc_verify/run_vivado directory.

Note

In Linux paths the separator is /, while in Windows paths it is \. Vivado's TCL only accepts the Linux form, so be sure to remember to wrap paths in braces {} under Windows!

2.Use the source command to run the create_project.tcl script and wait for the Vivado project to be created; the project file is loongson.xpr under the minicpu_env/soc_verify/run_vivado/project/ directory. 

source create_project.tcl

3.Once the project has been created, be sure to check that the project Top is set correctly, that the simulation time is long enough, and whether the IP cores need a version upgrade.

How to upgrade the IP cores

After you create the project, you will see a red lock symbol next to the IP cores. This means that the Vivado version that created the current IP cores is older than the one you are using. Right-click and click upgrade IP to upgrade the IP cores.

Simulation length

When the simulation in Vivado stops after running for only 1000ns, increase the simulation time of the Vivado project as shown in the figure below. You can switch to units such as ms and s!

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text: Read and understand the code provided in the lab environment, and complete the missing parts of the code so that the design passes simulation and board verification.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the miniCPU project in the minicpu_env/soc_verify/run_vivado/ directory.
  2. Re-customize inst_ram in the miniCPU project and select the coe file from the corresponding func directory (minicpu_env/func/inst_ram.coe).
  3. Run the simulation of the miniCPU project (once the simulation window is open, just click run all) and start debugging. You can modify the switch value in the minicpu_tb.v file in the minicpu_env/soc_verify/testbench/ directory to check whether the led output matches what you expect (you must re-run the simulation after every change to the switch value). (The test program for this lab is a Fibonacci program: the Fibonacci sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …, and from the third term onward every term equals the sum of the two terms before it. The third term of the sequence is taken to be f(1), that is, f(1)=1, f(2)=2, f(3)=3, f(4)=5, … . Changing the DIP switch value is equivalent to changing n, and the led output gives f(n).)
  4. Once the myCPU simulation passes, synthesize and implement the design, generate the bitstream, and verify it on the board.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The simulation passes with the given test program, and the led output matches the correct value of the Fibonacci program.
  • After running on the board, changing the DIP switch value shows the correct Fibonacci result on the leds.

docs.title: Lab 6: Single-Cycle CPU with Twenty Instructions
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition 4.2 Verifying a Single-Cycle CPU with 20 Instructions / 4.3.2 Practical Task 6

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Extend the single-cycle CPU from five instructions to 20, covering a complete subset of arithmetic, logic, shift, comparison, branch, and memory access instructions.
  • Master the organization and workflow of the mycpu_env lab environment.
  • Learn to use an automated debugging method based on trace comparison, and use the func functional test programs to verify that your CPU is correct.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
From here on we will use the mycpu_env environment, and all the later labs take place in that folder. You do not have to master all of this right away — just pick up new material as the labs progress. The parts of the mycpu_env directory that are not listed here are irrelevant to the current practical tasks and will be introduced in the corresponding later labs.

The upgraded lab environment lives in the top-level subdirectory mycpu_env, and its directory structure together with a brief description of each part is shown below: 

|--gettrace/                The part that generates the reference trace.
|  |--src/                  Design source directory.
|  |  |--tb_top.v           Simulation top level; this module captures debug information into golden_trace.txt.
|  |  |--soc_lite_top.v     Top-level file of SoC_Lite.
|  |  |--refCPU/            The reference processor core design that produces the comparison trace.
|  |  |--CONFREG/           The confreg module, used to access the CPU and board peripherals such as the seven-segment display and the DIP switches.
|  |  |--BRIDGE/            A 1×2 bridge module: the CPU's data sram interface accesses confreg and data_ram at the same time.
|  |--gettrace.xpr          Vivado project file.
|  |--golden_trace.txt      The reference trace generated by running the func test program. You must generate it yourself.
|
|--func/                    Functional verification test programs used by the lab tasks.
|  |--include/              Directory holding the header files shared by the functional verification test programs.
|  |  |--sysdep.h           Header file holding some macro definitions common to GCC.
|  |  |--asm.h              Header file holding some macro definitions needed by LoongArch assembly, such as LEAF(x).
|  |  |--regdef.h           Assembly mnemonic definitions of the 32 general-purpose registers under the LoongArch32 ABI.
|  |  |--cpu_cde.h          Macro definitions of SoC_Lite-related parameters, such as the base address of the confreg that accesses the seven-segment display.
|  |  |--inst_test.h        Header file of macro definitions used by the verification programs for each functional test point
|  |--inst/                 Assembly program files for each functional test point.
|  |  |--Makefile           The Makefile in this subdirectory, which is invoked by the Makefile in the parent directory.
|  |  |--n*.S               Verification programs for each functional test point, written in assembly.
|  |--obj/                  Directory holding the compiled functional verification test programs
|  |  |--*                  See the description in a later section.
|  |--start.S               Boot code and main function of the functional verification test.
|  |--Makefile              Makefile script that compiles the functional verification test programs
|  |--bin.lds               The result of compiling bin.lds.S; it can be removed with the make reset command
|  |--convert.c             C source code of the tool that generates the coe and mif files
|
|--myCPU/                   The RTL code of your own CPU.
|
|--soc_verify/              The SoC system verification environment for your own CPU
   |--soc_dram/             The verification environment for when the CPU's external interface connects to distributed RAM.
   |  |--rtl/               SoC_Lite design source directory.
   |  |  |--soc_lite_top.v  Top-level file of SoC_Lite.
   |  |  |--CONFREG/        The confreg module, used to access the CPU and board peripherals such as the seven-segment display and the DIP switches.
   |  |  |--BRIDGE/         A 1×2 bridge module: the CPU's data sram interface accesses confreg and data_ram at the same time.
   |  |  |--xilinx_ip/      Customized Xilinx IP, including clk_pll, inst_ram, and data_ram.
   |  |--testbench/         Functional simulation verification platform.
   |  |  |--mycpu_tb.v      Functional simulation top level; this module captures debug information and compares it against golden_trace.txt.
   |  |--run_vivado/        The run directory of the Vivado project.
   |     |--constraints/    Design constraints for the Vivado project.
   |     |--mycpu_dram_prj/ Directory holding the Vivado project files.
In Lab 6 we only need the mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_dram directory! The project-creation script is also in the corresponding run_vivado folder, and it is used in the same way as in Lab 5, so we will not repeat that here.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
We have already provided a single-cycle CPU supporting five instructions. Please extend that CPU to implement the following 20 instructions:

  • Arithmetic: add.w, sub.w, addi.w
  • Comparison: slt, sltu
  • Logic: nor, and, or, xor
  • Shift: slli.w, srli.w, srai.w
  • Memory access: ld.w, st.w
  • Branch and jump: jirl, b, bl, beq, bne
  • Other: lu12i.w

Select EXP6 as the test program

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The configuration of this lab environment is rather involved, so work through it carefully. The other three environments under soc_verify are configured in the same way.

  1. Open WSL2 and go to a Linux shell, then enter the mycpu_env\func directory and run make EXP=6; the 6 here selects the test program for Lab 6.
  2. Open the gettrace project — mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr. (The IP cores in this Vivado project were created with Vivado 2019.2; if you open it with a newer version of Vivado, upgrade the IP cores as described in Lab 5 environment section.) Run the gettrace project's simulation (once the simulation window is open, just click run all and wait for the simulation to finish) to generate a new reference trace file golden_trace.txt (mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt). The simulation has to run to completion before golden_trace.txt holds its complete contents, so check by hand that golden_trace.txt is not empty.
  3. Go into the mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_dram/run_vivado/ directory and start the project that verifies myCPU. If no project has been created in that directory yet, use the create_project.tcl script there to create one.
  4. Re-customize the inst_ram IP in the project.
  5. Run the simulation in the myCPU verification project (once the simulation window is open, just click run all), and verify and debug the design until the simulation test passes (a passing simulation test prints PASS!, while a failure prints the PC of the first instruction where your design differs from the reference core).
  6. Synthesize and implement the design in the myCPU verification project, generate the bitstream, and verify it on the board.
Accessing Windows folders from WSL2

Just prefix the path with /mnt/, and note that you must use the / separator! 

# Go to your user directory on the C: drive
cd /mnt/c/Users/<your-username>

# Go to the Desktop
cd /mnt/c/Users/<your-username>/Desktop

# Go to a project folder on the D: drive
cd /mnt/d/projects/myapp

Re-customizing inst_ram

Whenever we update the func program and recompile it, we need to re-customize inst_ram so that it picks up the latest contents of the func/obj/ directory.

Note that only the projects under soc_verify need inst_ram re-customized; for the project under gettrace, the INST_COE macro in soc_lite_top.v points directly at the mif file in the func/obj/ directory. The procedure for re-customizing inst_ram is as follows:

In the Sources window, find the inst_ram IP, then double-click it or right-click and choose "Re-customize IP…" to open the customization view. In the re-customize IP dialog that appears (shown in Figure 4.7), select the Other Options tab, tick Load Init File, and under Coe File click "Browse" to select the newly generated inst_ram.coe, then click OK. In the Generate Output Product window that appears, click Generate (choose global or ooc mode as needed) to finish re-customizing inst_ram.

golden_trace and difftest

At the moment we take a correct core, run the same test program on it and generate a golden_trace.txt file, then compare that against our own core; if the two match exactly, we can consider that our core ran the corresponding test program correctly.

However, using golden_trace to verify core correctness is no longer widely used; these days core correctness is more often verified by differential testing (Difftest). Students who are interested can read the XiangShan processor's official documentation for a detailed introduction to DiffTest

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
• Refer to the LoongArch32R Reduced Instruction Set Manual to implement the instructions the lab requires.
  • Pay attention to signal bit widths, and avoid bizarre bugs caused by signals being truncated!!!

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 6 test program passes simulation in full, and the simulation prints PASS;
  • After running on the board, both LEDs are green and the seven-segment display shows 1400 0014;

How to tell a correct board run

When verifying on the FPGA there is only one way to judge whether the result is correct. The correct behavior of the test program is:

1.At the start, all the monochrome LEDs are off, the bicolor LEDs show one red and one green, and the seven-segment display shows all zeros;

2.During execution, all the monochrome LEDs are off, the bicolor LEDs show one red and one green, and the high and low 8 digits of the seven-segment display count up together;

3.At the end, all the monochrome LEDs are off, both bicolor LEDs are green, and the high and low 8 digits of the seven-segment display hold the same value, corresponding to the number of functional test points — for example: 3A 00 00 3A.

If an error occurs while the test program is running, the first point at which the high and low 8 digits of the seven-segment display differ is the number of the functional test point that failed, and the final state is: all the monochrome LEDs lit, both bicolor LEDs red, and the high and low 8 digits of the seven-segment display holding different values.

In addition, you can adjust the execution speed of the program by changing the DIP switch value, so that you can see the seven-segment display count up in full.

docs.title: Pipelined CPU Design
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

The labs in this section correspond to Chapter 5, Simple Pipelined CPU Design and Chapter 6, Adding Ordinary User-Mode Instructions to the Pipeline of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition.

Getting Started with Chisel

From this section onward, the CPU is developed in Chisel instead of Verilog. Work through the Getting Started with Chisel notes to set up your Chisel development environment and learn the basic syntax.

In Lab 6 we already used Verilog to build a single-cycle CPU supporting 20 instructions. Next we will implement a five-stage pipelined CPU.

A five-stage pipeline splits the single-cycle datapath into the five stages IF / ID / EX / MEM / WB, joined by pipeline registers. Instructions execute in parallel across the stages, raising throughput several-fold — but dependencies and hazards come with it.

The labs in this section build a five-stage pipeline framework first (Lab 7), then resolve hazards with stalling and forwarding (Labs 8 and 9), and finally extend the instruction set (Labs 10 and 11).

docs.text: Lab Topic Reference in the Book Lab 7: A Simple Pipelined CPU Without Hazard Handling Build the five-stage pipeline framework 5.1.1 Practical Task 7 Lab 8: Resolving Hazards with Stalls Detect dependencies and insert pipeline bubbles 5.1.2 Practical Task 8 Lab 9: Resolving Hazards with Forwarding Eliminate some stalls with a forwarding network 5.1.3 Practical Task 9 Lab 10: Arithmetic, Logic, Multiply and Divide Instructions Extend the ALU instruction group and the multiply/divide unit 6.1.1 Practical Task 10 Lab 11: Branch and Memory Access Instructions Extend branch/jump and load/store instructions 6.1.2 Practical Task 11

docs.title: Lab 10: Adding Arithmetic, Logic, Multiply and Divide Instructions
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition 6.1.1 Practical Task 10: Adding Arithmetic, Logic, Multiply and Divide Instructions

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Add arithmetic and logic instructions and multiply/divide instructions to the pipelined CPU you already have.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
This practical task asks you to build on the CPU you implemented in Lab 9 and do the following:

Add the arithmetic and logic instructions: slti, sltui, andi, ori, xori, sll, srl, sra, pcaddu12i.

Add the multiply and divide instructions: mul.w, mulh.w, mulh.wu, div.w, mod.w, div.wu, mod.wu.

Multiply and divide are multi-cycle operations

32-bit multiply and divide cannot complete in a single pipeline cycle, so you need a separate multi-cycle multiply/divide unit and must freeze the pipeline while it operates. Pay attention to how it interacts with the stall and forwarding logic: multiply/divide results must also feed into the forwarding network.

Select EXP10 as the test program

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Copy the code of the CPU you implemented into the mycpu_env/myCPU/ directory.
  2. Edit the func configuration file, mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h, to select the exp10 configuration, then compile it. (make EXP=10)
  3. Open the gettrace project, mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr. Run the gettrace project's simulation (once the simulation window is open, just click run all and wait for the simulation to finish) to generate a new reference trace file golden_trace.txt (mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt). The simulation has to run to completion before golden_trace.txt holds its full contents.
  4. Go into the mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_bram/run_vivado/ directory and start the project that verifies myCPU. If no project has been created in that directory yet, use the create_project.tcl file there to create one. If a project created for the previous practical task already exists there, you can open it and then refresh the list of CPU implementation files in the project.
  5. Re-customize the inst_ram IP in the project.
  6. Run the simulation in the myCPU verification project (once the simulation window is open, just click run all), and verify and debug the design until the simulation test passes.
  7. Synthesize and implement the design in the myCPU verification project, generate the bitstream, and verify it on the board.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 10 test program (n1~n36, 36 feature points in total) passes simulation.
  • On the board, both bicolor LEDs are green and the seven-segment display shows "2400 0024".

Implementation Hints

  • Check the encoding and semantics of each instruction one by one against the LoongArch32R instruction set manual;
  • For signed division, note that the quotient is truncated toward zero; implement the divide-by-zero and overflow cases (such as 0x80000000 / -1) as the manual specifies;
  • While the multiply/divide unit is operating, the stall control in the pipeline can reuse the logic from Lab 8.

docs.title: Lab 11: Adding Branch and Memory Access Instructions
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition 6.1.2 Practical Task 11: Adding Branch and Memory Access Instructions

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Add branch instructions and memory access instructions to the pipelined CPU you already have.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
This practical task asks you to build on the CPU you implemented in Lab 10 and do the following:

Add the branch instructions: blt, bge, bltu, bgeu.

Add the memory access instructions: ld.b, ld.h, ld.bu, ld.hu, st.b, st.h.

Byte enables

  • ld.b/ld.bu/ld.h/ld.hu must be sign/zero extended after the read; st.b/st.h must generate the correct byte write enable on data_sram_we and must not disturb the other bytes of the same word.

Select EXP11 as the test program

docs.text:

  2. Edit the func configuration file, mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h, to select the exp11 configuration, then compile it. (make EXP=11)
  3. Open the gettrace project, mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr. Run the gettrace project's simulation (once the simulation window is open, just click run all and wait for the simulation to finish) to generate a new reference trace file golden_trace.txt (mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt). The simulation has to run to completion before golden_trace.txt holds its full contents.
  4. Go into the mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_bram/run_vivado/ directory and start the project that verifies myCPU. If no project has been created in that directory yet, use the create_project.tcl file there to create one. If a project created for the previous practical task already exists there, you can open it and then refresh the list of CPU implementation files in the project.
  5. Re-customize the inst_ram IP in the project.
  6. Run the simulation in the myCPU verification project (once the simulation window is open, just click run all), and verify and debug the design until the simulation test passes.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 11 test program (n1~n46, 46 feature points in total) passes simulation.
  • On the board, both bicolor LEDs are green and the seven-segment display shows "2E00 002E".

Implementation Hints

At this point the CPU supports 46 user-mode instructions in total. Once you are done, we suggest you go through the decode table and confirm that every instruction's control signals (write-back enable, ALU operation, immediate type, memory access enable, branch decision) are complete and free of conflicts.

docs.title: Lab 7: A Simple Pipelined CPU Without Hazard Handling
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition 5.1.1 Practical Task 7: A Simple Pipelined CPU Without Hazard Handling

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Split the single-cycle CPU datapath into the five stages IF / ID / EX / MEM / WB, inserting pipeline registers between them.
  • Understand the throughput gain a pipeline brings and the price it charges (hazards).
  • This lab deliberately does not handle dependencies or hazards, so that you can see the resulting failures for yourself.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Warning

Before you start, make sure you have set up your Chisel development environment as described in the Getting Started with Chisel notes and that you have a basic grasp of Chisel syntax.

docs.title: Vivado Project Environment
docs.text:
Warning

The lab environment still lives under mycpu_env/, but for verification you no longer use the soc_dram/ subdirectory — use the soc_bram/ subdirectory instead!

Because the instruction RAM and data RAM the CPU accesses are now implemented as block RAM rather than distributed RAM, the lab environment has to be adjusted as well: it is still the mycpu_env environment, and the gettrace/, func/, and myCPU/ subdirectories keep their locations and purposes unchanged. The only difference is that under soc_verify/ you no longer use the soc_dram/ subdirectory but the soc_bram/ subdirectory instead; the files inside soc_bram/ are organized along the same lines and serve the same purposes as those inside soc_dram/. The directory structure of the adjusted lab environment and a brief description of each part are shown below: 

|--gettrace/                The part that generates the reference trace.
|--func/                    Functional verification test programs used by the lab tasks.
|--myCPU/                   The RTL code of your own CPU.
|--soc_verify/              The SoC system verification environment for your own CPU
   |--soc_bram/             The verification environment for when the CPU's external interface connects to block RAM.
   |  |--rtl/               SoC_Lite design source directory.
   |  |  |--soc_lite_top.v  Top-level file of SoC_Lite.
   |  |  |--CONFREG/        The confreg module, used to access the CPU and board peripherals such as the seven-segment display and the DIP switches.
   |  |  |--BRIDGE/         A 1×2 bridge module: the CPU's data sram interface accesses confreg and data_ram at the same time.
   |  |  |--xilinx_ip/      Customized Xilinx IP, including clk_pll, inst_ram, and data_ram.
   |  |--testbench/         Functional simulation verification platform.
   |  |  |--mycpu_tb.v      Functional simulation top level; this module captures debug information and compares it against golden_trace.txt.
   |  |--run_vivado/        The run directory of the Vivado project.
   |     |--constraints/    Design constraints for the Vivado project.
   |     |--mycpu_bram_prj/ Directory holding the Vivado project files.

From Lab 7 onward, both the instruction RAM and the data RAM are implemented with block RAM, so accesses to them have to be qualified with a chip-select signal. The myCPU top-level interface therefore gains a chip-select signal for the instruction RAM, inst_sram_en, and a chip-select signal for the data RAM, data_sram_en. Both are 1 bit wide and active high.

To meet the needs of the later practical tasks, inst_sram_we and data_sram_we in the myCPU top-level interface both change from 1 bit to 4 bits, and their meaning changes from a RAM write enable to a RAM byte write enable.

docs.title: Lab 9: Resolving Hazards with Forwarding
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition 5.1.3 Practical Task 9: Resolving Hazards with Forwarding

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Use forwarding (forward) to improve how data dependencies are handled, reducing stalls and raising pipeline efficiency.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
This practical task asks you to build on the CPU you implemented in Lab 8 and do the following:

Add appropriate data forwarding paths to reduce stalling.

load-use dependency

The data of a load instruction does not arrive until the end of the MEM stage, while the instruction right behind it needs that data in the EX stage — forwarding cannot cover this one-cycle gap, so a load-use dependency still requires a one-cycle stall. Almost all other results produced by the ALU can be resolved by forwarding.

Select EXP9 as the test program

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:

docs.title: Exceptions and Interrupts
docs.text:
Read the explanatory part of the corresponding chapter of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition first, then come back to these lab notes for the lab requirements and work through them.

Warning

All lab requirements are governed by the lab notes on this site. Do not follow the lab requirements given in CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition!

Reference in the Book

The labs in this section correspond to Chapter 7, Support for Exceptions and Interrupts in CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition.

Exceptions and interrupts are the cornerstone of a CPU's support for an operating system: system calls, page faults and timer interrupts all reach the kernel through this one mechanism. The labs in this section add precise exceptions to your pipelined CPU: capturing the processor state at the point of the exception accurately and handing control to the exception handler.

docs.title: Lab 12: Adding System Call Exception Support
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 7.1.1 Practical Task 12: Adding System Call Exception Support

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Add CSR registers and CSR access instructions to the CPU, implement the syscall system call exception and the ertn return from exception, and support the complete trap—handle—return loop.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
In this practical task you build on the CPU you completed in Lab 11 and do the following:

  • Add the CSR access instructions to the CPU: csrrd, csrwr, csrxchg, ertn.
  • Add the control status registers to the CPU: CRMD, PRMD, ESTAT, ERA, EENTRY, SAVE0~3.
  • Add the syscall instruction to the CPU, implementing support for the system call exception.

Precise Exceptions

Exception response requirements: when an exception occurs, ERA records the PC of the instruction that triggered it, ESTAT records the exception code (Ecode 0x0B for syscall), the privilege level switches to PLV0, and the PC jumps to EENTRY; ertn restores the PC from ERA and returns. Several instructions in the pipeline may carry an exception flag at the same time, so you must guarantee that "the effects of instructions before the exception take effect and the effects of instructions after it do not".

  • On the board both bicolor LEDs are green, and the seven-segment display shows "2F00 002F".

Implementation Hints

  • The address of each CSR and the meaning of each field are as given in the LoongArch32R instruction set manual;
  • csrwr must return the old value to rd at the same time as it writes the new value; csrxchg exchanges bits one by one according to the mask in rj;
  • A CSR write and a later csrrd that reads the same register number are dependent on each other, so make sure this works together with the forwarding and stalling logic.

docs.title: Lab 13: Adding Support for Other Exceptions
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 7.1.2 Practical Task 13: Adding Support for Other Exceptions

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Add support for more exceptions and interrupts to the CPU, completing the precise-exception framework.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
In this practical task you build on the CPU you completed in Lab 12 and do the following:

  • Add exception support to the CPU: instruction fetch address error (ADEF), address misalignment (ALE), breakpoint (BRK), instruction not found (INE).
  • Add interrupt support to the CPU: 2 software interrupts, 8 hardware interrupts and the timer interrupt.
  • Add the control status registers to the CPU: ECFG, BADV, TID, TCFG, TVAL, TICLR.
  • Add the counter read instructions to the CPU: rdcntvl.w, rdcntvh.w, rdcntid.

When to Take an Interrupt

Interrupts are asynchronous events, but they must be taken at an instruction boundary, without interrupting an instruction that has already entered the pipeline. A common approach is to tag the instruction with a "carries an interrupt" flag as it is fetched; if the interrupt is still pending when that instruction commits, the CPU responds to it as it would to an exception, and the instructions behind it are flushed. Whether an interrupt is enabled or masked is decided jointly by CRMD.IE, ECFG.LIE and ESTAT.IS.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 13 test program (n1~n58, 58 feature points in total) passes in simulation.
  • On the board both bicolor LEDs are green, and the seven-segment display shows "3A00 003A".

Implementation Hints

  • Each exception is detected at a different point: ADEF during instruction fetch, INE/BRK during decode, and ALE during memory access (ALE must also record the offending address in BADV). The exception flags need to travel along with the pipeline stages and be arbitrated in instruction order at the commit point;
  • Timer: TCFG configures the timer and selects its period, TVAL reflects the current count, and TICLR is used to clear the timer interrupt.

docs.title: AXI Bus Interface
docs.text:
Read the explanatory part of the corresponding chapter of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition first, then come back to these lab notes for the lab requirements and work through them.

Warning

Reference in the Book

The labs in this section correspond to Chapter 8, AXI Bus Interface Design in CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition.

In a real system the CPU is not wired directly to memory; it interacts with the outside world through a bus protocol. The labs in this section move from a custom SRAM-like bus to the AXI protocol, and introduce random-delay verification.

docs.text: Lab Topic Reference in the Book Lab 14: Adding SRAM-Like Bus Support Turn instruction-fetch and memory-access requests into handshake-based bus requests 8.1.1 Practical Task 14 Lab 15: Adding AXI Bus Support Implement the AXI channel protocol and an SRAM-like-to-AXI conversion bridge 8.1.2 Practical Task 15 Lab 16: Completing AXI Random-Delay Verification Verify functionality and freedom from deadlock under random bus delays 8.1.3 Practical Task 16

docs.title: Lab 14: Adding SRAM-Like Bus Support
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 8.1.1 Practical Task 14: Adding SRAM-Like Bus Support

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Convert the CPU's external SRAM interface into an SRAM-like bus interface with a handshake mechanism, so that the CPU can tolerate memory-access waits.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Warning

The verification environment for this lab no longer uses the soc_bram/ subdirectory — use the soc_hs_bram/ subdirectory instead!

Now that the instruction RAM and data RAM the CPU accesses have changed from ordinary block RAM to block RAM with a handshake mechanism, the verification environment has been adjusted accordingly: the gettrace/, func/, and myCPU/ subdirectories keep their locations and purposes unchanged; the only difference is that under soc_verify/ you now use the soc_hs_bram/ subdirectory, whose files are organized along the same lines as those in soc_bram/:

|--mycpu_env/                Root directory of the lab environment.
|--gettrace/                 The part that generates the reference trace.
|--func/                     Functional verification test programs used by the lab tasks.
|--myCPU/                    The RTL code of your own CPU.
|--soc_verify/               The SoC system verification environment for your own CPU
   |--soc_hs_bram/           The verification environment for when the CPU's external interface connects to handshaking block RAM.
      |--rtl/                SoC_Lite design source directory.
      |  |--soc_lite_top.v   Top-level file of SoC_Lite.
      |  |--CONFREG/         The confreg module, used to access the CPU and board peripherals such as the seven-segment display and the DIP switches.
      |  |--BRIDGE/          A 1×2 bridge module: the CPU's data sram interface accesses confreg and data_ram at the same time.
      |  |--ram_wrap/        The RAM module wrapped in an SRAM-like interface.
      |  |--xilinx_ip/       Customized Xilinx IP, including clk_pll, inst_ram, and data_ram.
      |--testbench/          Functional simulation verification platform.
      |  |--mycpu_tb.v       Functional simulation top level; this module captures debug information and compares it against golden_trace.txt.
      |--run_vivado/         The run directory of the Vivado project.
         |--constraints/     Design constraints for the Vivado project.
         |--mycpu_hs_bram_prj/ Directory holding the Vivado project files.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
In this practical task you build on the CPU you completed in Lab 13 and do the following:

  • Change the CPU's external interface to an SRAM-like bus interface: on top of the existing sram interface signals, add the handshake signals inst_sram_addr_ok, inst_sram_data_ok, data_sram_addr_ok, and data_sram_data_ok. Once a request has been issued, it may take several cycles for a response to arrive, and the CPU pipeline must be able to freeze correctly while it waits.
  • Complete the random-delay functional verification of the func program for exp14 in the SoC verification environment built on handshaking block RAM.

Random delay

The RAM access delay in the verification environment is random (generated by a pseudo-random number generator in confreg.v). In simulation the initial random seed is specified by the RANDOM_SEED macro in confreg.v; on the board it is specified by the DIP switch state sampled during reset. Make sure your CPU works correctly under any delay.

Select EXP14 as the test program

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Update the code of your CPU implementation into the mycpu_env/myCPU/ directory.
  2. Edit the func configuration file, mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h: select the exp14 configuration and compile. (make EXP=14)
  3. Open the gettrace project, mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr. Run the simulation of the gettrace project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all and wait for it to finish) to generate a new reference trace file, golden_trace.txt (mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt). The simulation has to run to completion before golden_trace.txt holds its full contents.
  4. Go to the mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_hs_bram/run_vivado/ directory and launch the project that verifies myCPU. If no project has been created in that directory yet, use the create_project.tcl file there to create one.
  5. Re-customize inst_ram in the project.
  6. Run the simulation in the myCPU verification project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all) and verify and debug the design until the simulation passes.
  7. Run synthesis and implementation in the myCPU verification project, generate the bitstream file, and verify on the board.
Board verification requirements

On the board you should "toggle the DIP switches at random and then press reset", and the CPU must pass the 58 feature points of the func program for exp14.

The DIP switch state during reset serves as the initial random seed and determines the number of random delay cycles for instruction fetch and memory access. The CPU's execution state differs greatly from seed to seed, and hitting an error under some particular seed is very common. If you find that "the simulation passes but the board does not", set RANDOM_SEED in confreg.v to the failing seed value and reproduce the failure in simulation to debug it. When running on the board you should cover all three delay types as far as possible — long delay, short delay and no delay (for the mapping between seeds and delay types, see Figure 8.1 in the book).

After reset the DIP switches serve a second purpose: controlling the rate at which the seven-segment display accumulates, so that you can adjust the pace at which you observe the test.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 14 test program (n1~n58, 58 feature points in total) passes in simulation.
  • On the board both bicolor LEDs are green, and the seven-segment display shows "3A00 003A"; the design also passes for several different random seeds (toggling the DIP switches and pressing reset repeatedly).

Board verification requirements
