docs.title: Lab 16: Completing AXI Random-Delay Verification
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 8.1.3 Practical Task 16: Completing AXI Random-Delay Verification

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Refine the AXI bus interface design and verify the CPU's functionality and the robustness of its handshake under random bus delays.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
In this practical task you build on the CPU you completed in Lab 15 and do the following:

Refine the AXI bus interface design so that it completes the random-delay functional verification of the func program for exp16 in the AXI-based SoC verification environment; it must pass both simulation and board verification.

Why random delays expose bugs

A fixed-delay response masks handshake timing problems: bugs such as READY arriving late, VALID being de-asserted at the wrong moment, or data being lost during a multi-cycle wait only come to light once the delay is randomized. The random delay is generated by the pseudo-random number generator in confreg.v, and in simulation its initial seed is controlled by the RANDOM_SEED macro.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Update the code of your CPU implementation into the mycpu_env/myCPU/ directory.
  2. Edit the func configuration file, mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h: select the exp16 configuration and compile. (make EXP=16)
  3. Open the gettrace project, mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr. Run the simulation of the gettrace project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all and wait for it to finish) to generate a new reference trace file, golden_trace.txt (mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt). The simulation has to run to completion before golden_trace.txt holds its full contents.
  4. Go to the mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/run_vivado/ directory and launch the project that verifies myCPU. If no project has been created in that directory yet, use the create_project.tcl file there to create one.
  5. Re-customize axi_ram in the project.
  6. Change the RANDOM_SEED macro in mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/rtl/CONFREG/confreg.v to a different value, then run the simulation in the myCPU verification project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all) and verify and debug the design until the simulation passes.
  7. Repeat the previous step several times; the values you set for the RANDOM_SEED macro must cover all three random delay types (long delay, short delay and no delay).
  8. Run synthesis and implementation in the myCPU verification project, generate the bitstream file, and verify on the board.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 16 test program (n1~n58, 58 feature points in total) passes in simulation, and several sets of RANDOM_SEED covering the three delay types all pass.
  • On the board both bicolor LEDs are green, and the seven-segment display shows "3A00 003A".
Board verification requirements

On the board, func must run correctly every time you "toggle the DIP switches at random and then press reset" (the DIP switch state during reset serves as the initial random seed). If you see the "passes in simulation but fails on the board" phenomenon, debug it as described in Lab 14: write the failing seed into RANDOM_SEED in confreg.v and reproduce the failure in simulation; if it cannot be reproduced, look for coding-standard problems in your code, or use the Vivado logic analyzer for in-circuit debugging.

docs.title: Memory Management Unit (TLB)
docs.text:
Read the explanatory part of the corresponding chapter of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition first, then come back to these notes for the lab requirements.

Warning

The lab notes on this site are the authoritative statement of all lab requirements. Do not follow the lab requirements given in CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition!

Reference in the Book

The labs in this section correspond to Chapter 9, Memory Management Unit Design of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition.

Operating systems need virtual addresses: process isolation, demand paging and shared memory all depend on them. The MMU is responsible for virtual-to-physical address translation, and its core component is the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer).

In this section you will first build a standalone TLB module, then wire the TLB instructions, CSRs and exceptions into the CPU.

docs.title: Lab List
docs.text: Lab Topic Reference in the Book Lab 17: TLB Module Design Build a standalone TLB: lookup, replacement and maintenance instructions 9.2.1 Practical Task 17 Lab 18: Adding TLB Instructions and CSRs tlbsrch/tlbwr/tlbfill plus CSRs such as ASID and TLBIDX 9.2.2 Practical Task 18 Lab 19: Adding TLB-Related Exception Support TLB refill/invalid/modified exceptions, supporting kernel startup 9.2.3 Practical Task 19

docs.title: Lab 17: TLB Module Design
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 9.1 Analyzing the TLB Module Design / 9.2.1 Practical Task 17: TLB Module Design

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Design and implement a standalone TLB module, and complete module-level verification.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Warning

The verification environment for this lab is different from the SoC environments you have used so far. It is a standalone verification environment for the TLB module, located in the mycpu_env/module_verify/tlb_verify/ directory, and it does not use the func tests.

|--module_verify/            Module-level verification environment
   |--tlb_verify/            TLB module-level verification environment.
      |--rtl/                Design sources: the TLB module and the verification top level.
      |  |--tlb_top.v        Top-level file for the TLB module-level verification.
      |--testbench/          Functional simulation sources.
      |  |--testbench.v      Simulation top level.
      |--run_vivado/         Run directory for the Vivado project.
         |--constraints/     Design constraints for the Vivado project.
         |--tlb_prj/         Directory holding the Vivado project files.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
This practical task asks you to:

  • Design the TLB module. The RTL file must be named tlb.v and the module must be named tlb. For the input and output ports, follow the interface defined in section 9.1 of the book (two lookup ports, a TLBSRCH lookup, the TLBWR/TLBFILL write ports, the TLBRD read port, and INVTLB operations).
  • Verify your TLB using the TLB module-level verification environment, passing both the simulation and the board verification.

Design notes

  • The lookup uses a fully associative parallel comparison: every entry is compared against the incoming VPPN/ASID at the same time to produce a match vector, and the information of the matching entry is selected onto the output by a multiplexer;
  • The comparison must account for both the G bit (global entries ignore ASID) and the page size (a 4MB page compares only the upper 10 bits of the VPPN, while a 4KB page compares all 19 bits);
  • 16 entries are recommended (parameter TLBNUM = 16).

Aligning the top level with a Chisel BlackBox

Use a BlackBox to reference tlb.v, matching the port names to module tlb word for word, declaring and connecting clk/rst explicitly, and use HasBlackBoxResource to pull in the Verilog source file where necessary.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Finish the design and RTL of the TLB module and save it as tlb.v, then place tlb.v in the mycpu_env/myCPU/ directory.
  2. Go to mycpu_env/module_verify/tlb_verify/run_vivado/tlb_prj/ and open the project that verifies the TLB. If no project has been created there yet, use the create_project.tcl file in that directory to create one.
  3. Run the simulation in the TLB verification project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all) and debug until the simulation passes.
  4. Synthesize and implement the TLB verification project, generate the bitstream, and run the board verification.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The TLB module-level simulation passes (16 writes, 16 reads and 26 lookups in total; PASS!!! is printed once all of them are correct).
  • The TLB works correctly on the board.
Judging the simulation result

The simulation performs 16 writes, 16 reads and 26 lookups, and prints PASS once all of them have completed, as shown below:

    [   2705 ns] OK!!!write
    …………
    =========================================================
    Test end!
    ----PASS!!!
If the simulation reports an error, debug it. Inspect the accesses on the TLB interface to understand what the request is meant to do, then check whether the data read out of the TLB matches the expected result.

Judging the board verification result

When you run it on the board, the seven-segment displays report the progress of each stage in turn:

  1. Write (W): the rightmost seven-segment display counts up from 0x00 to 0x0f, and the rightmost single-color LED lights up when it finishes;
  2. Read (R) and lookup (S0/S1) run at the same time: the second display from the right (R) counts up from 0x00 to 0x0f; the second display from the left (S0, even-numbered requests) counts up from 0x00 to 0x18 in steps of 2; the leftmost display (S1, odd-numbered requests) counts up from 0x01 to 0x19 in steps of 2;
  3. When everything has finished, the three LEDs on the right light up, and a successful run reads 0x19180f0f on the displays. Stopping at any other value means the board verification failed.

docs.title: Lab 18: Adding TLB Instructions and CSRs
docs.text:

Implementation hints

docs.title: Lab 19: Adding TLB-Related Exception Support
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 9.2.3 Practical Task 19: Adding TLB-Related Exception Support

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Add the TLB-related exceptions and virtual-to-physical address mapping to the CPU, completing the full functionality of the MMU.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
This practical task builds on the CPU from Lab 18 and asks you to:

  • Add the TLB-related exceptions to the CPU: TLB refill exception, page invalid exception for load/store/fetch operations, page modified exception, and page privilege level violation exception.
  • Add the DMW CSRs to the CPU.
  • Add virtual-to-physical address mapping to the CPU.

Address translation modes

The DA/PG fields of CRMD select the translation mode: in direct mapping (DA=1) the address is mapped directly according to the DMW register configuration; in page mapping (PG=1) the virtual address is first looked up in the TLB to obtain the PPN, which is then concatenated into the physical address. TLB exceptions are detected in instruction fetch (IF) and memory access (MEM) — earlier in the pipeline and far more frequent than syscall and the like — so they must be folded into the precise-exception arbitration framework you built in Labs 12 and 13.

Select EXP19 for the test program

If no project has been created there yet, use the create_project.tcl file in that directory to create one. If a project from the previous practical task already exists there, you can open it and then update its list of CPU implementation files.
  5. Re-customize axi_ram in the project.
  6. Run the simulation in the myCPU verification project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all) and debug until the simulation passes.
  7. Synthesize and implement the myCPU verification project, generate the bitstream, and run the board verification.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 19 test program (n1~n72, 72 function points in total) passes in simulation.
  • On the board both bicolor LEDs are green, and the seven-segment displays read "4800 0048".

Implementation hints

  • Telling the exceptions apart: a TLB lookup miss → refill exception; a hit with V=0 → page invalid exception (you must also distinguish whether the access came from an instruction fetch or a data access); a store that hits with D=0 → page modified exception; the current PLV lower than the entry's PLV → page privilege level violation exception;
  • The virtual address that triggered the exception is recorded in TLBRBADV (which differs from the general-purpose BADV);
  • For the exception entry address (EENTRY, or the dedicated TLB refill entry) and the way ertn restores DA/PG, follow the LoongArch32R instruction set manual.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Read the explanatory part of the corresponding chapter of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition first, then come back to these notes for the lab requirements and complete them.

Warning

The lab notes on this site are the authoritative statement of all lab requirements — do not refer to the lab requirements given in CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition!

Reference in the Book

The labs in this section correspond to Chapter 10, Cache Design of CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition.

The speed gap between the CPU and main memory is measured in orders of magnitude. A cache exploits the principle of locality to make the CPU faster, shortening the time the CPU spends stalled while it waits for data from main memory.

In this section you will first implement a standalone cache module (with an AXI bus interface and a miss-handling state machine), then integrate an ICache and a DCache into the CPU, and finally add the CACOP instruction for cache maintenance.

docs.title: Lab List
docs.text: Lab Topic Reference in the Book Lab 20: Cache Module Design Standalone cache: set associativity, miss state machine, AXI interface 10.1 / 10.2.1 Lab 21: Integrating the ICache into the CPU Hooking an ICache into the instruction fetch path 10.2.2 Practical Task 21 Lab 22: Integrating the DCache into the CPU Hooking a DCache into the memory access path and handling the store buffer 10.2.3 Practical Task 22 Lab 23: Adding the CACOP Instruction to the CPU Cache maintenance instructions: query and clean 10.2.4 Practical Task 23

docs.title: Lab 20: Cache Module Design
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 10.1 Cache Module Design / 10.2.1 Practical Task 20: Cache Module Design

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Design and implement a standalone cache module, and complete module-level verification.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Warning

The verification environment for this lab is not the SoC environment. It is a dedicated verification environment for the cache module, located under mycpu_env/module_verify/cache_verify/, and it does not use the func tests.

|--module_verify/            module-level verification environment
   |--cache_verify/          cache module-level verification environment.
      |--rtl/                design sources, including the cache module and the verification top level.
      |  |--cache_top.v      top-level file for cache module-level verification.
      |--testbench/          functional simulation sources.
      |  |--testbench.v      simulation top level.
      |--run_vivado/         run directory for the Vivado project
         |--constraints/     design constraints for the Vivado project.
         |--cache_prj/       directory holding the Vivado project files.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
The requirements for this practical task are as follows:

  • Design the cache module. The RTL file must be named cache.v and the module must be named cache. Apart from the clock input clk and the active-low reset input resetn, the input and output ports follow the definitions in Table 10.2 (interaction with the CPU pipeline over the SRAM-like bus) and Table 10.3 (read and write interaction with the AXI bus interface module) in Section 10.1 of the book.
  • Design specifications: 2-way set associative, 4 KB per way, 16-byte cache lines, LRU or pseudo-random replacement policy, hardware initialization recommended.
  • Verify your cache with the cache module-level verification environment, passing both simulation and board verification.

Key Design Points

  • Address split: virtual address bits [11:4] form the index (8 bits), physical address bits [31:12] form the tag (20 bits), and the in-line offset is 4 bits — that is, virtually indexed, physically tagged (VIPT) access;
  • The cache RAM must be customized by you: 2 blocks of TAGV RAM, 256×21 each; 8 blocks of DATA Bank RAM, 256×32 each (with byte write enable turned on; when customizing, do not tick "Primitives Output Register", so that data is returned in a single cycle);
  • Internally the module is organized around four kinds of access: Look Up, Hit Write, Replace, Refill, managed by a main state machine (IDLE/LOOKUP/MISS/REPLACE/REFILL) together with a write buffer state machine;
  • The data cache uses a write-back plus write-allocate policy; when a dirty line is replaced, it is written back to memory over AXI before the new line is filled in.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Complete the design and the RTL implementation of the cache module, save it as cache.v, and put cache.v in the mycpu_env/myCPU/ directory.
  2. Go to the mycpu_env/module_verify/cache_verify/run_vivado/cache_prj/ directory and open the project for verifying the cache. If no project has been created in that directory yet, create one using the create_project.tcl file there.
  3. Run the simulation in the cache module verification project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all) and debug until the simulation tests pass.
  4. Synthesize and implement the cache module verification project, generate the bitstream, and run the board verification.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The cache module-level simulation passes.
Interpreting the simulation results

Module-level verification starts at index=0. For each index it generates four random tag/data pairs. It first issues write requests to put those four values into the cache, and then issues read requests to read them back. If no error occurs in between, the index is incremented and a new set of tag/data pairs is generated for the same test, until the test for index==ff is complete.

For a write-to-cache request, the result the verification environment expects to see is this: after the write request is issued a Cache miss occurs, the cache module issues an rd request, and the verification environment returns all ones (0xFFFFFFFF). A write request may also trigger a replacement, in which case the verification environment compares wr_addr and wr_data against the tag/data combination described above, and the test aborts if the replaced value is wrong.

Once all the write operations are done, read operations follow, and the verification environment performs the same checks. After the cache returns the result of a read operation, the verification environment checks whether what it read is the same as what was written earlier.

During simulation, a write followed by a read is generated for four cache lines per index; when all the operations are complete, PASS is printed, as shown below:

    [   2705 ns] index 00 finishd
    …………
    =========================================================
    Test end!
    ----PASS!!!
If you find an error during simulation, debug it; the console prints the reason for the error. The verification environment only checks for data errors during replacement and for Cache read data errors.

Interpreting the board verification results

When running on the board, the leftmost two digits of the seven-segment display show the index of the test currently running, which increases step by step until it reaches 0xff, at which point the test stops.

Hardware Initialization

Because the CACOP instruction is not implemented until Lab 23, the cache must be initialized by hardware at this stage: when customizing the TAGV RAM, tick "Fill Remaining Memory Locations" and set the initial value to 0 (V=0 means every line is invalid), and implement the D table with registers so that it is simply cleared by the reset.

Implementation Hints

docs.title: Lab 23: Adding the CACOP Instruction to the CPU
docs.text:
Reference in the Book

CPU Design in Practice: LoongArch Edition, 10.2.4 Practical Task 23: Adding the CACOP Instruction to the CPU

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: • Implement the CACOP instruction (cache maintenance operations) in the CPU, the last piece of the Cache section.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Building on your work in Practical Task 22, this practical task asks you to do the following:

  • Add an implementation of the CACOP instruction to the CPU from Practical Task 22.

The semantics of CACOP

cacop op, rj, si12 performs a maintenance operation on the cache line (aligned to the line boundary) addressed by rj + sext(si12), selected by the op value: query (read the tag into a CSR), invalidate (clear V, discarding the data), write-back (write a dirty line back to memory), and flush (write-back plus invalidate). CACOP is a privileged instruction; executing it at any privilege level other than PLV0 raises a privileged instruction exception.

For the test program, select EXP23

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Copy the code of the CPU you have implemented into the mycpu_env/myCPU/ directory.
  2. Modify the func configuration file mycpu_env/func/include/test_config.h to select the exp23 configuration, and compile. (make EXP=23)
  3. Open the gettrace project, mycpu_env/gettrace/gettrace.xpr. Run the simulation of the gettrace project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all and wait for the simulation to finish) to generate the new reference trace file golden_trace.txt (mycpu_env/gettrace/golden_trace.txt). golden_trace.txt only holds complete contents once the simulation has finished.
  4. Go to the mycpu_env/soc_verify/soc_axi/run_vivado/ directory and open the project for verifying myCPU. If no project has been created in that directory yet, create one using the create_project.tcl file there. If a project created by an earlier practical task already exists there, you can open it and then update the list of CPU implementation files in the project.
  5. Re-customize the axi_ram in the project.
  6. Run the simulation in the myCPU verification project (once the simulation window opens, just click run all) and debug until the simulation tests pass.
  7. Synthesize and implement the myCPU verification project, generate the bitstream, and run the board verification.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• The Lab 23 test program (n1~n79, 79 functional points in total) passes simulation.
  • On the board both bicolor LEDs are green, and the seven-segment display shows "4F00 004F".

Implementation Hints

  • Once CACOP is implemented, the cache can be initialized in software: software initializes it simply by using CACOP to zero every tag, which makes the hardware initialization circuit a fallback;
  • While a CACOP is executing it may issue a bus write-back (flushing a dirty line), so the pipeline has to be frozen until it completes, just as it is for the multi-cycle multiplier and divider.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
To do good work, one must first sharpen one's tools. Before we formally begin the labs, some preparation is needed.

The lab environment for this course has three parts: Vivado, a WSL2/Linux environment, and the LoongArch32 cross-compilation toolchain.

docs.title: Vivado
docs.text:
Use a Vivado version 2019.2 or later; 2023.2 is recommended, as it noticeably speeds up simulation, synthesis, and implementation.

For a detailed Vivado installation guide, see: Installing Vivado

Tips for using Vivado

  • Windows builds of Vivado compile with 2 threads by default. Type the following command in the Tcl Console to enable 8-thread compilation and speed things up: set_param general.maxThreads 8
  • Synthesis and implementation are faster under Linux. If you have a physical Linux machine, consider installing the Linux version of Vivado.
  • Running Vivado inside a virtual machine is not recommended.
  • Do not use non-ASCII (Chinese) characters in the project path, and do not nest the project too deeply — creating the project directly under the root of a drive is recommended.
  • Do not use non-ASCII (Chinese) characters in your computer user name.

For the basic Vivado workflow (creating a project, running simulations, and programming the board), see the appendices of the book: Getting Started with Vivado and Advanced Vivado Usage.

docs.title: WSL2 / Linux Environment
docs.text:
We recommend using WSL2 with Ubuntu on Windows. The later labs require a Linux environment in which to compile the test programs.

Please look up a tutorial for installing WSL2 with Ubuntu on your own.

docs.title: LoongArch32 Cross-Compilation Toolchain
docs.text:
Compiling the func programs yourself requires the LoongArch32R GCC cross-compiler. You can download the toolchain package from LoongArch32 Reduced Cross Toolchain.

When downloading the package, choose the version matching your machine (X86 or LoongArch); the X86 case is used as an example below. **Download loongson-gnu-toolchain-8.3-x86_64-loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-v2.0.tar.xz ** into the Linux operating system's own file system. Note in particular that the X86 version of the LoongArch32R GCC cross-compiler currently supports only 64-bit systems (that is, systems where the uname -a command reports the architecture as x86_64). Then:

In the Linux environment:

(1) Open a terminal, change into the directory containing the archive, and extract it: 

sudo tar Jxvf loongson-gnu-toolchain-8.3-x86_64-loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-v2.0.tar.xz -C /opt/

(2) Then run: 

echo 'export PATH=/opt/loongson-gnu-toolchain-8.3-x86_64-loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-v2.0/bin/:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc && echo $PATH
(3) Open a new terminal and check the version of the la32r GCC cross-compiler: 
 loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-gcc -v
If the GCC version is printed correctly, the setup is complete.

docs.title: Lab Template
docs.text: This page explains how to obtain the lab template from GitHub and describes the structure and use of each directory. Please read through this page before starting the labs.

docs.title: Getting the Lab Template
docs.text:
The labs in this course are based on Loongson's official teaching lab environment cdp_ede_local, modified so that it runs correctly on the DIGILENT NEXYS 100T development board. The modified repository is at: cdp_ede_local

Clone it locally first. We recommend putting it under Windows, not inside WSL2.

git clone git@github.com:zihaojf/cdp_ede_local.git

Tip

We recommend that you manage your own versions carefully during development!

Once cloned, the repository root is structured as follows:

cdp_ede_local/
├── README.md          # Documentation: lab schedule and corresponding environments
├── dc_env/            # Labs 1-4: fundamentals of digital logic circuits
├── minicpu_env/       # Lab 5: single-cycle CPU with 5 instructions
└── mycpu_env/         # Labs 6-23: everything from the 20-instruction CPU onward

The three environments correspond to the three phases of the course labs. They are independent of one another and are used in sequence as the labs progress.

docs.title: dc_env (Labs 1–4)
docs.text:
dc_env/
├── exp1/    Running light
├── exp2/    Register file simulation
├── exp3/    Synchronous/asynchronous RAM
└── exp4/    Digital logic circuit design and debugging

Each expN directory comes with a source file skeleton, a testbench, and constraints (.xdc). Either open it directly in Vivado, or create a new project and add the source files. Your job is to complete/fix the source files, get the simulation passing, then run synthesis and program the board.

docs.title: minicpu_env (Lab 5)
docs.text:
minicpu_env/
├── func/           # Test programs: assembly → instruction memory initialization file
│   ├── start.S         # Fibonacci program (runs with only 5 instructions)
│   ├── Makefile        # Cross-compilation; produces inst_ram.coe / inst_ram.txt
│   └── inst_ram.coe    # Compiled instruction image (for simulation)
├── miniCPU/        # CPU RTL
│   ├── minicpu_top.v   # Single-cycle CPU top level
│   ├── regfile.v       # Register file
│   └── tools.v         # Helper components
└── soc_verify/     # SoC verification environment
    ├── rtl/            # soc_mini_top.v + CONFREG + xilinx_ip
    └── testbench/      # mycpu_tb.v: simulation top level

A minicpu capable of running five instructions is already provided. Run the simulation in the Vivado project under soc_verify: the CPU fetches instructions from inst_ram and executes the Fibonacci program in func, and the result is verified through the CONFREG (observed during simulation) or the seven-segment display (on the board).

docs.title: mycpu_env (Labs 6–23)
docs.text:
This is the environment you will use for most of the course; all subsequent labs are developed incrementally on top of it.

mycpu_env/
├── myCPU/              # Your CPU RTL
│   ├── mycpu_top.v     # CPU top level
│   ├── alu.v, regfile.v, decoder_*.v ...
├── func/               # The func functional test program suite
│   └── inst/           # n1-n79 per-feature test assembly (each file targets a few instructions)
├── gettrace/           # Reference trace generator (for trace-comparison debugging)
├── module_verify/      # Standalone module verification (Lab 17 TLB, Lab 20 Cache)
│   ├── tlb_verify/     # Lab 17: TLB module verification
│   ├── cache_verify/   # Lab 20: Cache module verification
│   ├── mul_verify/     # Multiplier verification
│   ├── div_verify/     # Divider verification
└── soc_verify/         # SoC verification environment, split into four directories by bus interface
    ├── soc_dram/       # Lab 6: distributed RAM interface (single-cycle)
    ├── soc_bram/       # Labs 7-13: block RAM interface (pipeline/exceptions)
    ├── soc_hs_bram/    # Lab 14: BRAM interface with handshake
    └── soc_axi/        # Labs 15-23: AXI bus interface

Two things to note

  1. The initial code in myCPU/ contains functional bugs. This is part of the lab design (find them and fix them), not a repository bug;
  2. Each lab corresponds to a different SoC directory under soc_verify — pay attention to which directory the simulation or board project uses.

Toolchain

The Makefile in func/ depends on the loongarch32r-linux-gnusf-* cross-compilation toolchain (needed when you compile the test programs yourself). For simulation and verification you usually only need the inst_ram.coe image shipped with the repository — just run it directly.

docs.title: Lab Environment Checklist
docs.text:
Before starting Lab 2, confirm each of the following:

  • Vivado ≥ 2019.2 is installed, and you can create a project and get a simulation running;
  • WSL2/Ubuntu is available, with the basic tools gcc, make, and git in place;
  • The LoongArch32 cross-compilation toolchain is installed and added to PATH;
  • You have set up your own code repository

Now let's start the labs!
